.Some hon. MEMBERS: Agreed.
IMr. ROSS (Souris): This has been a matter of considerable interest to me ever since I came here in 1940, and in various budget debates I have advocated a period of five years. I think that argument is sound, because I understand that in Britain, where they have not the hazards in agriculture that we have in parts of Canada, they do allow a five-year period. If that is so I think the minister and the department might well consider the point.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am advised that there is no averaging in the United Kingdom, that it was withdrawn in 1926.
Wrong again.
I am quite prepared to admit it if I am wrong. I understood that to be the case, and apparently it was at one time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have just been informed that this is so.

My own experience in western Canada has been much like that of the hon. member for Battle River. We certainly have our ups and downs; and while this is a step in the right direction I certainly would like to see the period made five years if possible, instead of three. I think it would
[The Acting Chairman.]
be much better for a successful agricultural programme and for the nation as a whole if the average could be taken over a five-year period, and I trust the minister will seriously consider whether he can see his way clear to amend the resolution accordingly. As I say, it is something we have asked for since at least 1940.
While I am on my feet I should like to ask a question in regard to another contentious matter, particularly in the ranching areas of western Canada. I refer to the question of allowing some exemption in connection with what is recognized as a breeding herd. I have looked through these resolutions very carefully, and I do not see any other place where that matter might be discussed. Various hon. members on both sides of the house have raised this question in previous years. The suggestion is that at least a percentage of the recognized breeding herd should be allowed as capital when the herd is sold. I do not see any provision in the resolutions which would specifically take care of that. As I understand the situation through force of circumstances, because of lack of feed or something of the kind, a man may have to sell within one year a herd of good cattle which he has spent his lifetime building up; and if he does so, what he receives must be shown as income. It is true that under section 17 he can average that income over three years, but still it is quite a hardship on the man who has made the raising of live stock his life's undertaking. I should like to think the minister and the department might find some way to give a little relief to ranchers of this description.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
On that particular point, as my hon. friend knows this is a question which has received the fairly continuous and active consideration of the tax department for some time. I do not know that any solution satisfactory to the cattle raisers has been found as yet; the question is under continuous examination, but I do not know that I can give any definite statement now as to what if any change will be made. I recall that the Minister of Finance made some reference to this matter in his budget speech, at page 2918 of Hansard, where he said:
The general adoption of the three year forward averaging system which I have just announced should be of great assistance in more normal cases where a live stock herd is being maintained but annual live stock sales may vary from year to year. Several suggestions for carrying the basic herd principle further have been made and in this connection I must acknowledge the help received from various members. Most of these, however, involve maintenance by the farmer of accounting records of greater or less complexity and whether they will prove practicable from the standpoint of both

Income War Tax
the farmer and the tax administration is a matter which will have to be worked out by the administrative officials in consultation with the Department of Agriculture.
I am advised that those discussions are still proceeding. I think it is clear that the proposed three-year average should afford some measure of relief, but I am not an expert in this field and my opinion on that, as on some other matters, is not of very great value.
Would the minister mind indicating to the committee what particular objection could be offered, from the government's point of view, to extending this to five years instead of three?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: One obvious objection, of course, is that the farmer would get no benefit for five years, since the averaging must be five years forward. One cannot average back, because the farmer's return may not have been filed. As contemplated under this resolution he would have to go forward. The number of years suggested is the average before the farmer can derive any benefit. In the case suggested by the hon. members for Battle River and Cariboo it would mean that the farmer would have to wait five years before getting the benefit of the averaging. The line has to be drawn somewhere. This, I suggest, is a substantial measure of relief, and it seems to me we should try it out. I should add that it is a moving average, in that it keeps moving forward. '

I approve the resolution as far as it goes. As the minister has already said, it does afford a measure of relief. I am sure however that the contention of the hon. members for Battle River and Souris can easily be justified. From time to time farmers have what are know as dispersion sales, when they sell off their stock and implements which they have accumulated over a good many years-perhaps ten or twenty. If they are to be allowed to average only over three years, then it is certainly unfair because such a sale would represent an accumulation of twenty years of effort. I do not wish to press the matter further, but I think the mechanics of this matter should be examined into. The minister stated a case where a farmer in one year made $7,000, in the next year $5,000 and in the next year $3,000. In the final year, averaging for the three years, he had only a small amount to pay by way of income tax. What would happen if those figures were reversed? Suppose he had more in two years than the three years would amount to; would he get a refund?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: He gets a refund.

I just wanted to be sure about
that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I intended to say that in my preliminary statement.

I did not hear it. The next thing I should like to find out from the minister is this. Let us take the year 1948, and average it up with 1947 and 1946. Does that complete the calculation or the averaging, so far as it goes? In the year 1949 could one use 1948 and 1947?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: He takes 1949, 1948 and 1947. That is what I meant by saying that it is a moving average.
He can use those years on two or three occasions.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes; it is a continuing three-year average.
I am glad to hear that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It seems to me that that largely takes away the need for the five-year average, once it comes up to the third year. It is a moving average, and, as the hon. member for Haldimand has so aptly said, one may use the same years two or three times in averaging.

I want to say something about this five-year average, because I have been sent to Ottawa by the constituency of Selkirk, in which are included both fishermen and farmers, and they want the five-year provision.
The last argument used by the minister was his best. But suppose we have to wait five years-if it is to be just and reasonable we do not mind waiting that time. I want to be sure that it is just and reasonable. I think five years is more reasonable than three. The minister has said that the process of spreading it over a number of years has been done away with in the old country. I would point out, however, that over there they have a crop every year. They do not have to wait five or six years, as we sometimes do in the west. I support the hon. members for Battle River and Souris when they urge that it be made five years.
While I am on my feet I should like to ask the minister for a clear definition of "farmer". I should like to be clear on that before I go back to Selkirk.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
This time I knew what I was going to say before I rose. While I should like to oblige my hon. friend by giving that definition, I do not feel I can do so in sufficiently adequate legal t:rms. The deputy minister tells me that consideration has been given this matter. It is a difficult problem,
Income War Tax

and we hope that when the bill is before the house within the next day or two, when we have completed these resolutions, it will contain a satisfactory definition of "farmer".

Can the minister define
"farmer"?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I would not attempt to define it to-day.
That is the kind of answer I expected from a lawyer. It does not answer my question at all.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: What I intended to say to the hon. member was that the bill which will follow the resolutions may contain a definition of "farmer". I am not capable of defining it.

"May" and "shall" are much the same. This is a serious matter. I am particularly concerned about my own constituency, because they sent me here. There are many different kinds of farmers in the Red River valley, and I would not like to see any of them left out. For instance, we have mink farmers. Would they be included? A mink farmer might have a good crop this year, but next year a dog with distemper may come around and the farmer might lose his whole crop. Is he to be taken into consideration? Then what about the market gardener when he loses his crop through flooding or a hail storm? Is he classified as a farmer?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The hon. member is pointing out the defects which are obvious to all of us when we attempt to frame a definition of "farmer". I am inclined to agree that we must attempt to do it in the act, although it will not be an easy task. I agree, too, that all classes of genuine farmers should receive the benefit of this proposal.

Has the Department of Finance given consideration to incomes on farms earned by the whole family? We know that income tax forms are filled out by separate individuals, whereas five or six individuals may have earned the income. This is most unfair to the farmer who has children ranging from ten to sixteen years of age who are going to school but who also milk cows and help at harvest and threshing time. There is nothing in the income tax act which allows anything for their wages. After they become sixteen years of age an allowance can be made for board and a certain amount of wages. Prior to that, however, although they add to the farmer's income, he must pay on it. Has anything been done about this?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I believe the ordinary rules would have to apply. An adult son of a

farmer could hire out to the neighbouring farmer as a helper. I can see no legal reason why he could not be paid by his father, and in such event the wages would be deductible as expenses of operation. The income of the farmer would be reduced proportionately while the income received by the son, let us say, would be taxable income if he were getting over the exemption limit.

I have not been able to get my point across. What the minister has told me is correct as applied to the young fellow who has reached sixteen years of age and is able to go and work for himself, but I am thinking of the farmer's wife and family, his sons and daughters, who are at home and who milk the cows and do the other jobs. There is no allowance made for that work, ?.nd the farmer has to pay on the income that is made by five or six different people. We all know that the wife on the farm contributes to the farm income by producing poultry, honey, and so forth. She works from morning to night, and no allowance on income is made.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: What my hon. friend has said is true, but the same thing is true of other occupations. In the small town where I was brought up the wife and children often helped, possibly around a small store or in the home. It is all part of a way of life, although it may be a bit more pronounced in the case of the farmer's wife.
In the case referred to by the minister they would work only from eight in the morning until the time came to close the store for the day, but the farmer's family would work from daylight to dark.

There are quite a number of sections which deal with these matters. Resolution No. 17 reads:
That a farmer or fisherman be permitted for the 1948 and subsequent taxation years, at his option, to compute his liability to pay tax on the average of his income for the taxation year and the two preceding taxation years.
If we are to make progress I think we shall have to stick to the resolution before the committee and deal with each resolution as we come to it.

I should like to follow up the remarks of the hon. member for Souris in respect to the unfair treatment of those who have sold herds over the past several years. I should like to cite an example which I have given before. There is one man in my riding who over the years has accumulated a good deal of land. Any profit which he made from his farming activities he put into more land. To-day his

Income War Tax
holdings are considered as capital gain. I know of several farmers in that same area who have built up large herds but who because of lack of help or difficulty in marketing have had to sell their herds. They have received most unfair treatment; to use a slang expression, they have lost their shirts. The man who had accumulated land over the years is considered to have a capital gain which is non-taxable, while the man who accumulated a herd and had to sell is taxed to the limit.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Of course that is true also in other fields. In the one case the man is putting his earnings into capital, while in the other case he is putting his earnings into inventory.
I consider that any man who builds up a herd over the years is making a capital gain.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: He charges to his annual income his expenses in building it up.
Surely a calf is a capital gain.

I should like to support the idea advanced by the hon. member for Battle River. I made the same suggestion when I spoke in the budget debate. The minister gave us a hypothetical case of a farmer wrho makes $7,000 this year, $5,000 the following year and $3,000 in 1048. That may be possible in the east, but it is not possible in the west. If a farmer in the west had an experience like that for three years I think he would be quite lucky. As the hon. member for Battle River pointed out, because of low temperatures that have prevailed during the last few days many farmers in the west will likely have nothing at all.
One farmer I know of had a loss in 1942- the income tax department acknowledged that loss-of $1,100. In 1943 he had an income of $2,500 upon which he was taxable. In 1944 he had a profit of a little over $1,100. In 1945, because of circumstances beyond his control, he had to sell $1,100 worth of cattle. Surely such a man is entitled to more than three years in which to average his income. The minister says that this is a sort of revolving affair, but I should think that if such a farmer averaged his income in 1948 he would be through and would have to start all over again.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I did not call it "revolving"; I called it a moving average. We are starting this in 1946; 1946, 1947, and 1948 will be the first three years which can be averaged. When the year 1948 is concluded and' the farmer
knows his results for that year, he will then be in a position to determine finally his income tax liability for the three years. He is entitled to have his average go on to 1949. In 1049 he takes the years 1947, 1948 and
1949,	so that he has the same two years in as he had in the preceding year. Then in 1950 he will have 1948, 1949 and 1950. It is a moving average.
Supposing he exercised his option in 1948 and averaged his income for the three years, would he be through?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No. In 1949 he has the option of averaging again, unless the law is repealed.

That puts a different
picture on the whole situation.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: If a man elects to average his income, the income of 1948 will affect the tax of 1946, the tax of 1947, the tax of 1948, the tax of 1949 and the tax of
1950.	In effect, when the thing gets going, the good year or the poor year will have its effect on the two preceding years and on the two following years. In reality there is an effect over five years.

There will be an averaging of even more than five years.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The income of the middle year affects that year itself and affects the two preceding years and the two following years.

I do not think there is going to be any difficulty about whether we average it on three or the five years, because the income tax department is so inefficient that my fishermen, on the coast have had no tax returns since 1942. The result is they will have a five year average before they are through. I have a letter here which I received from a cooperative in Prince Rupert and which I gave to the income tax department. It is dated April 26, and it points out that sixty-eight fishermen have a total of $21,365.75 being held back. As late as July 10, I received another letter to the effect that they are getting from the Vancouver office dozens of requests to file returns when in fact returns have been filed. I object strenuously to this inefficiency which is putting an unfair burden upon these people. I realize the department has helped out to the extent that it has cut down the amount taken from the fishermen When they sell their fish immediately from twenty per cent to ten per cent and from ten per cent to five per cent, depending on the type of fishing that is done. First, I

Income War Tax
should like to ask the minister wthy there is discrepancy between the east and west coasts; why is it you have to take off ten per cent and five per cent-it used to be twenty and ten per cent-on the west coast when you do not do it on the east coast? I have been on the fisheries committee and heard the canning companies say that the eastern fishermen are as prosperous as any fiAermen in the world. The men on the Pacific coast feel that they are being grossly discriminated against.
I have a suggestion to make to the department in the matter of collecting income taxes. In the halibut fleet on the west coast the men work on a Share basis with the skipper, and the boat also receives a share. The skipper owns the boat and he is taxed both as skipper and as owner of the boat. He feels that he should not be condemned, as it were, because He owns the boat, to have to pay two taxes. I would urge that a departmental income tax office be established in northern British Columbia to solve these problems because our people there are getting no satisfaction from the Vancouver office. The only reply I have had to my letter in regard to the reductions from twenty to ten and ten to five is that letters are still coming from the department asking for more returns. Would the minister consider setting up an income tax office in northern British Columbia? The difficulties have been going on since 1942 and time is rolling on.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I shall be very glad to
consider whether it would not be possible to open an office in northern British Columbia. On the other point as to discrimination, I will look into that. I do not see why there should be discrimination. Mind you, the deduction at the source must be taken care of, but I will concede that so far as I can see there should be no discrimination between the fishermen on the west coast and those on the east coast.

In connection with the three-year moving average, the point made by the minister that if the five-year period were adopted the farmer would have to wait for five years before getting any benefit is not generally applicable, for this reason. The farmers have in large degree shared the fairly high level of prosperity which has been general across the country and the farmers in my district at all events have been fifing returns for the last three or four years. If they were allowed to take into account their returns over the previous years there would be no necessity for their waiting a further five years 
before they could start to average. The Minister of Justice, in the figures which he just gave, I think lent point to the argument in favour of the five-year moving average as against the three-year. He pointed out that if we take the three-year period, the middle year affects the average for the two preceding and two subsequent years. If you take the five-year period, one year will affect the tax for the four preceding and the four subsequent years, and in that way you are more likely to get the real average. I think it is conceded that farming cycles run in at least ten-year periods, certainly not five, and therefore the greater number of years you take into account the nearer you get to the real average, certainly more so than if you take the three-year period. In addition, the five-year moving average was the recommendation of the Department of Agriculture itself. After receiving briefs from the council of Canadian beef producers, representing councils all across the dominion, the Department of Agriculture submitted a brief to the Department of Finance, in which they had this to say:
After careful study, the department makes two recommendations:
1. Taxes be finally assessed on the basis of a five-year moving average of profits and losses.
From the illustration they give on the second page of the brief it is quite clear that they intended it to be a five-year as against the current three-year proposal. At all events they recommended that it be a five-year period. Has the Department of Finance given consideration to that brief? Since the minister has said that he will give further consideration to this matter before to-morrow, I would ask if the Department of Finance has made specific objections to the point raised, and whether there is any reason why the five-year period should not be adopted.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Careful consideration was given to the brief, and it was felt that the three-year average was appropriate. This is a special right which is given to one class of the community. It has been urged for some time. I think myself that it is a step in the right direction. After careful consideration the Minister of Finance, his advisers and the government came to the conclusion that the three-year period was appropriate, and that is the proposal that is put forward in the budget resolutions.

It cannot be denied that it is a move in the right direction, but I hope the minister will between now and to-morrow consider this suggestion, which was first advan-

Income War Tax
ced by the member for Battle River, and see if it does not deserve further consideration.
On the point of the capitalization of breeding herds, it seems to me that this whole question comes down to whether a breeding herd or basic herd is capital.
I think that is hardly in order in this resolution.

The resolution deals with the liability of a farmer to taxation, and allows him to average his income over a three-year period. The question of the capitalization of the breeding herds comes in, Mr. Chairman because the farmer may sell all his herd and is liable to income tax on the proceeds. My point is that the three-year period is of no assistance to him.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think it would be appropriate, Mr. Chairman, for hon. members to discuss that point on the resolution now before the committee.

On the point of the capitalization of breeding herds, it seems to me that this whole question comes down to whether a breeding herd or basic herd is capital. The point behind the submissions advanced by those who want the basic herd regarded as capital is that the breeding herd is as much one of the tools of production as land and buildings or the tools used in a factory. I made this point last year when this matter was up for discussion, and I do not think anything is to be gained by repeating what I said then, but I wish to point out in addition that the United States Department of Finance does recognize the breeding herd as capital. The Canadian Department of Agriculture in its brief, in appendix 2, referred to the special treatment allowed in the United States and quoted the following extracts from the US. Inland Revenue Bulletin No. 11 of June 12, 1944:
Live stock used for draft, breeding or dairy purposes, irrespective of whether such stock was raised or otherwise acquired, is property used in the trade or business, of a character which is subject to the allowance for depreciation.
And further this extract is given from the United States Department of Agriculture, publication 554, dealing with farm bookkeeping and the federal income tax:
Depreciable capital goods-
Capital is the word used:
Depreciable capital goods includes all buildings and land improvements (except the owner's dwelling), machinery, equipment, work animals, breeding and dairy stock.
In the United States the breeding herd is regarded as capital. When this question was raised last year the Minister of National Revenue advanced certain arguments against such a view, which are to be found at page 3743 of Hansard of December 18 last. The minister made this point:
Again, it had to be pointed out that the cost of raising or purchasing that stock had been allowed as an expense of previous years . . .
The answer to that is that there are many allowances which are made for capital outlay. Reduction from income is allowed for capital acquisition, and yet when the asset is subsequently sold it is not claimed that the proceeds are income simply because the original allowance was made. All we wish to do is to draw the same parallel between these capital assets and capital assets represented by breeding herds.
Would the hon. member give an example of capital increase, as far as business is concerned, where the income tax department allows it?

Yes. Where a doctor lays out money to enlarge his library he is acquiring something which he uses in the course of his profession, and he is allowed a reduction in taxable income for the purpose. But if subsequently he sells his library, the proceeds of that sale are not regarded as income but as a realization of capital.
But that is a professional investment.

I think I know what the hon. gentleman has in mind, and I shall deal with the point in a moment, when I trace the parallel between allowance for depreciation and allowance for acquisition or replacement of breeding stock. That point was dealt with by the Minister of National Revenue at page 3744:
Questions have been raised as to the taxation of the proceeds of breeding animals. Inasmuch as the cost of purchasing or raising such animals has been allowed as an expense, the proceeds of sale represent taxable income.
As regards depreciation in business, a business is allowed to set aside a certain amount for the purpose before taxation; yet when the asset is sold the proceeds are not regarded as income simply because a deduction has been allowed for depreciation. In the same way, if you have to replace a breeding herd-because animals deteriorate over a passage of years; after a time an animal is no longer useful for breeding purposes-the fact that you have been allowed to make a
Income War Tax

deduction for replacement or to buy a new animal, which corresponds to depreciation, is no argument that when you sell your stock the proceeds of sale constitute income and not capital. The Department of Agriculture recognized that point in its brief, in which it stated:
Prices of pure-bred breeding stock are subject to extremes beyond reason, caused by influences outside of Canada and outside the agricultural industry proper and are the result of buying by wealthy men or hobby farmers; yet the bona fide breeder must pay such prices if he is to remain in business, although well aware that he is likely to experience a heavy loss.
That is an incontrovertible fact and, if taken into consideration, is a strong argument in support of the contention that breeding herds are capital. If that position is once recognized-and it is the true position; it is the basis of the argument-there can be no justification for any further delay in giving due recognition to the fact in the tax system. It is true the Minister of Finance pointed out, at page 2918, as referred to by the acting minister, that the general adoption of the three-year forward averaging system should be of great assistance, but he referred to the "more normal cases where a live stock herd is being maintained". That in itself shows that it is not applicable where the herd is being sold, because the moment you sell the herd your operation is completed. You cannot average forward, because you will not have sales in the succeeding year, although if the three-year system is adopted you can average back for two years. But the only effect of that will be that your tax in the two preceding years will be considerably raised, and the net effect is that no relief will be given the taxpayer at all.
Further support of this contention will be found in the second of the recommendations given in the brief of the Department of Agriculture, where it is urged that breeding herds be recognized as capital assets. The hon. member for Battle River, the hon.-member for Souris, the hon. member for Wentworth, and nearly all other hon. members who have spoken on this side, have given illustrations of how the failure to recognize this principle works injustice to the farmer. I know of numerous examples myself. The reason this point is important now is that farmers, and particularly cattle ranchers operating their business as a going concern, are paying taxes. Many of them are getting old and wish to retire but are prevented from doing so or, if they do retire, they are taxed 
on the proceeds of the sale of the whole herd, so that instead of having a fairly substantial amount on which to retire, they have little left and have to look about for some small business or other in which to engage.
The thing is a problem now and I suggest to the minister very earnestly that he lose no time in finding a solution. He should not content himself with saying that the matter is receiving active consideration by the department. If there is any basis of truth in the contention put forward, I submit to the minister that the time to make adjustments is now.

A short time ago an hon.
member asked the minister to define "farmer," and I understood the minister to say that he would give a definition later. I want to make this suggestion to him when he is having these definitions drawn up. To-day there is what is known as the aquafarmer, that is to say, the oyster farmer. That class of farmer comes under all the regulations of the fisheries department. Again there are fur farmers throughout Canada, and they all come under the regulations of the Department of Agriculture. I offer this suggestion to the minister in the hope that it will help him in the definition of " farmer."

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Thank you.

Some
time ago the Minister of Justice referred to the proposal that the farmer, at his option, be allowed to compute his income tax over a period of three years, and he said that the three-year period would really be covering a period of five years. That is so, but it does not meet the point that has been made by the member for Battle River. The important thing to the farmer is that he be allowed to compute his income tax over a period of five years, which is the recommendation of the Canadian federation of agriculture. Taking the three years 1947, 1948 and 1949, in 1947 the farmer would make his computation on the basis of 1947, 1948 and 1949. The point to be established in conformity with the amendment which the member for Battle River moved is that the farmer wants to be able to compute his tax over the average of five separate years.

Before we leave this point I wish to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. members for Souris, Selkirk, Wentworth, Kamloops and many others who have spoken with reference to the placing of herds in the capital assets class. We all realize that

Income War Tax
before a person can make any profits out of a herd he has to invest money in it, the same as in his farm buildings. In connection with the remarks made by the Minister of Justice, the hon. member who has just taken his seat has pointed out something that should be taken into consideration. You deal with 1946, 1947 and 1948. You get the average of these years and immediately you go on to the year 1949. You dispense entirely with the year 1946 and use the years 1947, 1948 and 1949, so that you are still on a three-year average.
One question has been asked of me on numerous occasions, namely, if the farmer is on the three-year average and uses it for a certain number of years, can he go back to the annual?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr. TOWNLEY-SMITH: On that particular point, can a farmer or fisherman duck around? Can he take three years on his option and then take one year, and then return to the three-year system and pick out the years which suit him best? Let me say a word on the five-year average which has been referred to by a number of speakers. When universities are considering their experimental work they invariably take a five-year average, or longer if possible. They feel that they can get closer to the truth by taking not less than five years, and more than that if at all possible. In five years you do actually come closer to the actual situation.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The five-year question is
under discussion at the moment, but I think it is evident to hon. members of the committee that once a farmer has elected to average his income, it is bound to be to his interest to continue on that basis. It cannot-be otherwise.

I should) like to say a word about the basic herd principle. We discussed it at some length on the budget resolutions last year, and hon. members gave numerous reasons why it should be adopted. At that time the minister said that it was being given and would be given active consideration. We have discussed it again to-day, and once more the minister has said that it is being given active consideration. Apparently no progress has been made; we are in exactly the same position now as we were last year. Has the government adopted the basic herd principle, and is it prepared- to put it into its taxation system?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The answer to that question is no.

Then my second question does not apply; I was going to ask, when. If the answer to the question is no, then the information given to us by the minister last year and this year is misleading. It was stated that the matter was being given active consideration. I say it is misleading particularly in view of the statement on page 2918 of Hansard, which the minister read this afternoon, and which certainly gave me the impression that the government was prepared to adopt the principle.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
No; what I intended to convey, and what the minister intended to convey, was that the question was and still is under consideration. It is a difficult question, and if I must answer categorically the question whether the government adopted what my hon. friend refers to as the basic herd principle, I must answer him by saying no.
Mr. ZAPL1TNY: I wish to support all that has been said about the matter of breeding herds. I appreciate what the minister says about the difficulty of working out the details in that regard. However, I have something here which I think is simple and easy to understand, and which will provide relief for farmers wbo raise live stock and live stock products. It has been sent to me by the cooperative live stock marketing association of Dauphin, an association which keeps me up to date on live stock matters. If I may I should like to read it for the consideration of the minister. It is as follows:
Whereas there has been a serious decline in the production of live stock and dairy products; and
Whereas Canada is in desperate need of these agricultural products to help feed the starving masses of Europe;
Therefore be it resolved that for the purpose of encouraging production of live stock and live stock products, amounts up to $1,000 gross income from the sale of live stock and live stock products be exempt from income tax.
It is based on a slightly different principle from that suggested in the discussion which has been going on, but there can be no question that it would be a simple and direct way to bring relief to those engaged in the live stock business.
Before I resume my seat I should like to refer to the mathematics which have been drawn up with regard to the five-year period. It is a fascinating subject, but I am afraid that the impression which was left by the Minister of Justice that this will mean a five-year average in the long run is not correct, at least, in my opinion it is not. I have
Income War Tax

worked it out on paper, and as I understand it this is the way it would work out. At the end of 1948 you would take the three years, 1916, 1947 and 1948, but in 1949, at the end of the taxation year, you would take the years 1947, 1948 and 1949. In 1950 you would take the years 1948, 1949 and 1950; in 1951, you would take the years 1949, 1950 and 1951, and in 1952 the years 1950, 1951 and 1952. That takes in five years, and if you examine the figures you will find that in no year does one year occur more than three times. If it does - not occur more than three times then automatically we must understand that the average is the three-year average. You could go on for a thousand years if you wanted to, but each year would occur only three times, and the average would be a three-year average. I think that should be clearly understood.

I had to be absent from the chamber and I do not know what took place in my absence. I should like to say that the suggestion to extend the period from three to five years for taxation purposes is a sound one. Every major farm organization has made submissions asking that this be done, which I think proves conclusively that the farmer believes it would be to his advantage.
There is another question that I should like to raise at this time; the hon. member for Bow River referred to it the other day. As the government knows, quota deliveries were established for the years 1941, 1942 and 1943. In 1944 the quotas were lifted, with the result that farmers were able to sell wheat which they had not been able to sell because of the quota in the years 1941, 1942 and 1943. A circular was sent around at that time and in addition was printed in the newspapers; I shall refer only to the first paragraph:
Where grain raised in one year is carried over, due to quota restrictions but for no other reason, and is sold in subsequent years, the proceeds of such sale may be treated as-
(1)	income of the year in which the sale took place, or
(2)	income of the year in which the grain was raised.
Farmers acted on that declaration in good faith. However, it was cancelled in 1945, but in view of the fact that the circular was sent out, the farmers were under the impression that grain raised in 1941, 1942 or 1943 and held back because of the quota and then sold in 1944 could be changed back into the year in which it was grown. Further, I have a letter sent me the other day by a man in the small town of Morrin who had been filling out returns for farmers. This is what the letter said:

I am herewith enclosing a letter received from the income tax department at Calgary, which is a vital issue regarding all farmers, as they were forced to hold this grain until 1944 from previous years owing to the quota set by the dominion government, also this is absolutely contrary to their promise of allowing the farmer to transfer his grain back to the year it was grown, and not have to include it in the year it was sold.
They mention cash wheat in this letter. Now all grain sold in 1944 was practically cash grain, as the farmer collected his money as soon as delivered. Also mainly all grain is sold on this basis and not on an instalment plan. So I cannot see that this statement has any bearing in this case.
The letter the farmer had received from the department stated that this could no longer be done. Here is the letter from the inspector of income tax:
Your letter of June 14 has been received, and in reply it may be stated that the reversion of cash wheat sales to apply in the year in which the wheat was grown is not allowable under provisions of the Income War Tax Act, where cash returns are filed.
I wonder if the minister could explain why, after issuing a statement such as I read, later they should refuse to allow the farmers to pay taxes on that basis. Certainly it does seem to be a breach of faith on the part of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I understand the answer to my hon. friend's question is that an incorrect ruling was given to one taxpayer and was circularized by that taxpayer.
Would the minister repeat that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I say an incorrect ruling was given to one taxpayer, and1 I understand it was circularized by that taxpayer. I am informed that is what happened.
This is not sent out by the taxpayer but by the government, and it refers to the Canadian wheat board producer certificates. This is n.ot circularized by the taxpayer but by the department.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am sorry; I thought my hon. friend was referring to a letter. I wonder if I could have a look at the circular he mentions. Now that my hon. friend has given it to me I see it does not indicate .who issued it, but perhaps if my hon. friend would let me have this I can look into it at the dinner recess and see if I can give him a more detailed explanation, later.

Following up the question asked by the hon. member for Calgary East and the reply thereto of the minister, which as I understand it was that the department does not accept the basic herd principle, let

Income War Tax
me ask this question. Is the department of the view that if a farmer sells his herd of cattle, which has been operated as a going concern for perhaps ten years, the proceeds of every animal sold should be regarded as income? Is that the view of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am advised that the answer to that question is yes, because the cost of each of the cattle raised has been treated as an expense by the taxpayer in previous years.

Does the minister or the department not admit any similarity or parallel between allowing expenses for purchases and operation in this case and allowing depreciation before taxation and deductions for other capital outlays in other businesses?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I thought I answered that question before by saying that the herd is part of the inventory of the taxpayer. If a trader or merchant increases his inventory out of earnings-well, I must confess I cannot see the parallel between depreciation of fixed assets and a herd of cattle, which is something that is growing from year to year.

But the point is that it is not growing. If it is operated as a going concern it remains stationary from year to year. A basic herd might be two hundred; the average increase might be fifty, and it is the average increase which is sold, while the basic herd remains the same. The minister said they were purchased out of income. Suppose a man inherits a ranch from his father. He did not get it out of income; it came to him as a capital asset. The breeding herd was there; the thing was a going concern. Certainly it was not purchased out of income. Or take the case of a man going into the business. He leaves some other form of activity; he cashes in on his capital assets there, sells his business and acquires perhaps
850,000	which he puts into a ranch and a herd. That is not bought out of income; it is capital. Yet if he sells the herd two years later he is taxed on it-that is, according to the principle enunciated by the minister. If he went on the inventory basis he might be safe; but on the principle enunciated by the minister he would be taxed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am afraid I am not competent to discuss details. Of course every taxpayer in that business is free to operate on an inventory basis. In my recollection this question has been discussed on the budget resolutions for the last two or three years. The same points, some of which may be very good, have been brought forward; and, as the minister said in his budget speech, the question is still being considered by the Department of National Revenue in consultation with the Department of Agriculture. Rightly or wrongly, they have not yet been able to find a solution, but they will continue to consult and I can assure my hon. friend that, the points which he and others have made to-day will not be overlooked.
May I just emphasize that this is done in the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We shall have a look at the United States practice and see.

When the hon. member for Kamloops was speaking a while ago I believe the hon. member for Halifax asked what other business could be allowed an expense and a write-off, and then sell their equipment or whatever it was as capital. I think that is done in almost every business.
Which would increase their capital surplus.

If a man sets up a manufacturing concern he is allowed to write off his equipment over a period of years. During the war it was three years; in other cases it is four or five years. Then if he sells that business and his equipment, he sells it as capital; there is no argument about that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: If there is anything left to-sell.

Yes; and there generally is. I know where a farmer buys a new power tractor he is allowed to write it off over five years. If he is a good operator and keeps it in good shape, it may last considerably longer than that. One of the reasons given f by the Minister of Finance for allowing the 12J per cent increase in the prices of farm implements was that these used tractors were selling for more, at farm sales to-day, than they cost when new. That was the minister's own argument; yet the operator was permitted to depreciate them over five years, after which they were allowed as capital. I am prepared to admit that this is a difficult problem, to be quite fair about it, but I certainly do think some arrangement should be arrived at under which it would be acknowledged that a breeding herd is capital rather than inventory, as the acting minister says. If you put up a building you are allowed your depreciation; when you sell it it is acknowledged to be capital. About a year ago I understood that following consultation between the Department of Finance and the Department of Justice, based upon the recommendations of the federation of agriculture, some solution
Income War Tax

was practically arrived at under which certain basic years were to be taken for the basic herd, as is done for this averaging period now. I should think you could have a basic year when a man had actually purchased his breeding stock, and develop it from that time on.
I am really quite serious about this matter. I believe the man who is raising live stock as Ihis chief means of income should have his basic herd recognized by the department as capital. The whole trouble is a question of definition by the Department of Finance alone as to wlhat should be considered inventory and what should be considered capital. Certainly, as the minister says this matter has been debated ever since I came here in 1940, and as I say, I understood some solution had been agreed upon by negotiation between the. Department of Agriculture and the Department of Finance. I trust that may be so in fact before too long.

May I make one comment on this, merely to reinforce what has been said by the hon. member for Souris? I do feel that this is a high priority question for the department. I believe I realize the difficulty, because I have had some acquaintance with a couple of cases where the matter was under consideration in a somewhat important way. What struck me-and this is not offered by way of criticism, or with any intent to criticize-was that so far as I could make out there was still a great lack of precision and definiteness in the method, which was used. That was the impression I got from the two cases which came to my attention. I do suggest that this matter ought to be. given high priority.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: As the hon. member realizes, one cause of difficulty is, to use his words, lack of appreciation in the method of accounting of taxpayers.

So as to correct an impression created by a statement by the hon, member for Souris with respect to depreciation, may I point out that the average commercial firm doing business sets up its balance sheet, its profit and loss statement. Further, it must show its assets and liabilities. From liabilities deducted from assets it will Show its surplus. That must indicate each year, to the satisfaction of the income tax branch, what its earning power is. It is true there is an opportunity for the man in business to write off a certain depreciation. For a brick building it is 2i per cent; for a wooden building 5 per cent, and for fixtures 10 per cent, covering a period of ten years. So far as I know, except in special cases during the period of fMr. J. A. Ross.]
the war, there is no such thing as a writeoff of the entire amount in three years. I think hon members should understand that clearly. The largest amount in the average commercial business-is 10 per cent on fixtures, whereas in respect of property it is 2| per cent and 5 per cent. If an individual piece of machinery is purchased, that would be capital expenditure. There is no allowance made for expenditures in that connection. During the war, by order in council, those who had fuel oil equipment for heating their buildings were ordered to do away with that and to instal coal equipment. They were not permitted immediately to write off the cost of the coal equipment which they were obliged to put in in order to cany out the regulations.
It could be depreciated over a number of years.

But not in anything like two or three years, That change did not go the full five years; it was something like two or three years. One had to take out the equipment and lay it aside, and he had less than thirty cents on the dollar on his investment. Thus there was a distinct loss to the average business man.
You have no biological increases in your business.

In regard to merchandise, the market price was often used in connection with the increased price of goods. The minute one began to write down, an income tax inspector would check up very closely. I do say to the income tax branch officials, however, that in the change-over from oil to coal the branch should have been much more generous in the matter of depreciation.

I would underline the urgency of this matter, because it was only a few weeks ago that the hon. member for Stanstead drew attention to the large number of dairy cattle that were being exported. Depreciation in the herds results in part from the ceiling price on butter. The same condition exists in British Columbia, where dairy cattle are being sent out of the country, and where heifer calves are being killed off because of the ceiling price on butter. If breeding herds cannot be regarded as capital, it means that another handicap is added to the farmer.

The matter of introducing depreciation into the question whether a basic herd is capital, or whether it is not just beclouds the issue. The simplest way to look at it is this. Two men, we will say, came to Alberta twenty-five years ago. Each of whom had $2,000. One bought 100 acres

Income War Tax
of land at $20 an acre; the other bought 100 cows at $20 a head. Each man spent $2,000 of capital. Assuming that neither increased his holdings, twenty-five years later both are reasonably old men and wish to retire. Because of the appreciation in land values the man with 100 acres may sell at S100 an acre, and will have no income tax to pay on it. The man with the 100 cows will sell them at $100 each, along with the rest of his herd, and must pay an income tax on his return. If he sells the rest of his herd at the same time, it means that the total amount he receives in one year is large, and the tax rate is high. What actually happened was that most men of that kind increased their holdings. To return to the example I have mentioned, one would end up with a'thousand acres of land and the other with a thousand head of breeding stock. As the amount increases, the injustice increases in ratio to the amount each man receives. I believe this example states the condition about as simply as it can be stated. The matter is most urgent, because large numbers of men want to retire, and if they do so they are at a disadvantage. They find that the herds they have built up over a lifetime are of no great advantage, because if in one year they sell out their herds, a large amount of their life savings is wiped out in income tax. This is an injustice against the cattle producer, who should not be at a disadvantage as compared with the grain farmer or anybody else. As I said earlier, instead of simply considering the matter the government should forthwith make a definite decision.

This provision dealing with earned income was extended a few years ago to farmers and fishermen. In my opinion there should be equality of the general principles of taxation among all classes of our population. I remember when the principle behind this resolution was introduced, whereby farmers and fishermen could take an average. That principle of taxation had its beginning in what was known as the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, introduced by my former leader for farmers and extended afterwards to fishermen. I pointed out at that time that if the principle of -that legislation was extended to fishermen it should also be extended to industrial workers who might have jobs today but not to-morrow, especially in depression years such as we had in the thirties. The time [DOT]has come when the whole system of taxation should be revised, because, as is well known, down to a year ago farmers and fishermen were practically exempt from income tax.
I can tell you this, that the time has come when income tax should be restored to where it was from 1867 down to 1917. At that time it was still the prerogative and function of the municipality. What has been the result? In 1917 Sir Thomas White said that for one year in order to finish the war there would be a federal duplicate income tax, but the government has held on to the whole principle ever since that date. The time is coming when the principle should be changed and income tax restored to the municipalities.
If you are going to permit by this resolution farmers and fishermen to divide up their income and average it over a number of years, 1946, 1947 and 1948, the same privilege should be extended to other classes in the community, to civil servants, industrial workers and white-collar workers who may not be sure of their jobs and who will not be sure of their jobs if the small business men are continually taxed to death. The tax has to be collected by somebody; but there should be equality of treatment, otherwise the principle is all wrong. It amounts now to confiscation of property. These small retailers and wholesalers cannot pay a tax of 22 per cent, 32 per cent, 42 per cent-the rate goes up every year. If we pass resolution 17, what are we going to do next year? You are actually suggesting a principle that will never be applied because you are going to have to change the whole thing as to what the fishermen and farmers will pay in 1947 and 1948.

I have had many letters from stockmen in the Cariboo objecting to the matter that is being discussed. If a merchant were to sell his stock and go out of business, would he have to pay income tax on the entire amount received?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That is a question which I have attempted four or five times to answer this afternoon. As the law now stands, he would pay a tax on the entire proceeds of the sale on the ground that it is a sale of inventor)'. The discussion this afternoon has been instructive and informative. To some extent it is a repetition of the discussion which took place in previous years, but among other things it has served to bring out the great difficulty which is inherent to this question and which some of the hon. members who have spoken have admitted. I am advised that no longer than a week before the resolutions were brought in, a meeting took place between officials of the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Finance with the idea of still further working out the problem. I cannot add to what I have said
Income War Tax

to-day and to what the minister said in his budget speech. The question has not yet been solved, but we have not given up hope.

In view of the fact that there is some shade of admission on the part of the minister that there is a real difficulty here and also that there is a sort of undercurrent of suggestion that possibly there is some measure of injustice to farmers wiho desire to sell off their stock, would it not be wise to hold up this particular method of taxation for this year? It would be better for the state to suffer a little loss than to impose what seems to me a serious loss upon the individual farmer or cattle man.
While I am on my feet may I say I recognize the improvement the government is making in respect to spreading the tax on farmers over a three-year period. However, I must confess that it is not as good as it might be. I understand that this afternoon we are discussing resolution 17 in the hope that the government will give it further consideration and possibly bring in, to-morrow or some other day, some modification of the present policy. If that is the understanding I do not think much good can be served by saying anything more on the matter.
I think all points have, been pretty well brought out, but I wish to emphasize these two points. The man who wants to give up his cattle business and sells his stock should not be taxed on the entire amount he receives. Next, taxation on farmers generally should be spread over a five-year period. I hope the Acting Minister of Finance will accede to the wishes of the committee and give this matter a little more consideration. If he does that I am hopeful that there will be some modification in connection with these two points.

The minister said a few minutes ago that a discussion had been going on between officials of the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Finance in connection with this question of basic herds.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: With the Department of National Revenue.

I suggest to the acting minister and to the government that before any more conferences are held the government make up its mind whether it is going to adopt the principle. If the government accepts the principle that a basic herd is capital, then I suggest that there will not be a great deal of difficulty in working out some practical means of putting it into effect.
[*Mr. Abbott.]

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The stock breeder's herd would fee built up out of income. It would be very simple if we accepted initially the herds as they exist to-day, but I think that would be unfair to other taxpayers.	.

Certain breeding herds were built up out of income, but largely at times when the income tax was not applied so heavily. That is why the matter has become so important. The income tax is now quite high and something should be done about the matter. When I used the illustration a little while ago of 100 cows and 100 acres of land I had hopes that when I sat down the minister would either agree or disagree that the cows were capital. I should like to have his view on that matter.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is a difficult hypothetical question. Of course, from one point of view they could be considered as capital. My hon. friend went back a long way and cited the case of a man who bought 100 cows and the other man who bought 100 acres of land. I presume the man who bought the 100 cows has lived off the fruits of those cows ever since, but my hon. friend did not indicate what the man who bought 100 acres of land has been living on. The question is not very simple. The matter of dispersal sales is not directly involved in this resolution, but I think it was proper to discuss it and I so indicated. In my memory this subject has been discussed for the last four or five years. As I said a moment ago, the discussion has been very full and most informative. It has been carried on by hon. members who have personal knowledge of what they are speaking about, and may I say at once that I do not include myself in that group because I have had very little experience with breeding herds, although some years ago I did learn how to milk a cow. I do not know that much more can be added to what I have already said. The government will continue to give the most careful consideration to the representations which have been put forward and will carry on with their efforts to see if some acceptable solution can be found for this admittedly difficult problem.

I bought a farm a year ago, and two months afterwards I was offered twenty-five per cent more than I paid for it. I did not sell it because I did not buy it for that purpose. But if I had I would have gained because I would not have been taxed for it. If I had bought cattle and sold them I would have been taxed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: Are you in the farming business or in real estate?

In the farming business.

Income War Tax

I am not sure that this angle has been fully considered. Suppose a farmer has been building up over a number of years a dairy herd and eventually finds himself in a position where he has to change his methods of farming. Perhaps he is not able to go on milking cows because of lack of help or for some other reason, so that he sells his herd and pastures cattle on his land. Surely in a case of that kind his herd ought to be considered as capital. He has to use the money he got for his herd to buy cattle to put on his pasture. To me it does not seem right that the farmer should be taxed on everything he gets from the dispersal of ms dairy herd.

The minister has the Minister of National Revenue beside him and the deputy minister. I would ask him two questions about this blue form which the farmer has to use in making his income tax return. First, would the minister please explain how the income tax department computes the amount to be inserted in the form for produce raised on the farm and consumed on the farm? Second, would the minister explain why sales of wood, stone, lumber, trees, sand and soil off a farm are regarded as income? That comes under the heading of miscellaneous sales.
Mr. MoCANN: The farmer himself in making his return usually computes the value of the produce raised and consumed on the farm. With regard to the sale of gravel, sand or any other commodity from the farm, he puts that down as income when making his return. It is a source of revenue to the farm and as such is returnable as income.

Surely the minister does not pretend that once a sand or gravel pit on the farm is exhausted the farmer could grow another one. A contractor will come in and take perhaps
20,000	yards of gravel from the pit and then the pit may be exhausted. I do not think that could be classed as income.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: In that case we are out of farming and into mining.
No. The sales have to be entered on this special form for the farmer. I am sure the minister will not contend that soil or sand or gravel sold off a farm should be classed as income.
He is allowed depletion for it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
My remark about out of farming and into mining was semi-facetious. The farmer must account for the gravel sold
as part of his gross income; but, as the hon. member for Stanstead has pointed out, he can claim depletion, and if the depletion operates in the ordinary way he will in due course write off the entire value of his gravel or sand pit and pay no more tax with respect to it.

I do not regard as satisfactory the answer of the Minister of National Revenue as to the value to be inserted in the form of the produce raised and consumed on the farm. My experience has been that the local inspector tells the farmer what he has to put down there, so' much for the farmer, his wife and one child, let us say. Is that correct, or is it left to the farmer to compute the amount of produce consumed by him and his family at, say S100? My experience is that that is not accepted by the inspector, who says: We will put down $300 for that. And that is what the farmer has to pay. Has the farmer the right to say how much it is and put that down on his return?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: The farmer is supposed to make his own return. If we find that his return is not in keeping with the average return made by other farmers in that district, the department can raise the amount put down for that item.
What is the average amount inserted for that item in an average farming community where they are carrying on mixed farming?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: One cannot say that a certain figure would be constant for all communities. The figure used in the particular instance my hon. friend mentions would be the figure which is generally given and accepted in a return from that district.
What figure does the minister refer to, $100 or $150?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: Did not the hon. member mention $300 for three people?

No; I said $150. If the minister contends that his department charges $150 for the produce raised and consumed on the farm he does not know very much about how the farmer lives to-day. Why charge up eggs, milk, butter or anything like that when there are hundreds of people who keep the odd cow or a few chickens, and they do not have to account for what they raise in that way? To-day practically all that a farmer buys in the way of food is meat, and if you charge him $100 for that, that is far too much. I say that the
Income War Tax

arbitrary attitude adopted by the local inspectors is hardly consistent with the remarks of the minister.

I am sure there is no place on that form for the farmer to make a claim for depletion. I have a splendid wood lot on my farm and a gravel pit at the other end. Anything I receive from the wood or gravel sold has to be shown as income, and there is no place on the form for claiming depletion. If I sold the whole farm, including the wood lot and the gravel pit, the whole would show as capital, but the wood or gravel I sell has to be shown as income.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Technically the question* of wood is a little difficult. Strictly speaking, I think a man would be allowed to deduct depletion for wood sold from off his farm, and I am positive that he would be able to claim depletion on gravel sold from his gravel pit. As the hon. member for Stanstead has said, the farmer can claim depletion. I am not familiar with the particular form the farmer uses and do not know whether it contains a space for that, nevertheless the farmer is entitled to claim depletion.

In the study that has been made of this problem, has what is being done in other agricultural countries been considered? For instance, I understand that in Norway and Sweden the timber cut is com sidered as a crop. It is not an annual crop but is cut periodically and constitutes revenue. In those countries, is it charged up as income to the farmer? In great farming countries like the United States, have they found a solution for this particularly involved and annoying problem?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I cannot answer my hon. friend from personal knowledge. The officials of the Department of Finance especially charged with the investigation of these tax questions have the taxing systems of all other countries under constant review. As the committee knows, the farming community as a class are not large income tax payers and have not been in the past. Until very recent years, only a limited number was taxable or at any rate filed returns. Perhaps I had better make a brief explanatory statement. This resolution deals with the tax position of investment corporations. For the purpose of tax treatment, investment corporations are divided into two groups; that is, those with funded indebtedness and those without funded indebtedness. The latter group, those without funded indebtedness, are at present exempt completely from the excess profits tax, and the present proposal is that they shall be exempt in future from corporation income tax. It is believed that investment trusts of the sort being considered represent in effect merely collective investment by individuals, and it is considered that the mere funnelling of income through the company to individuals should not bring on an extra tax. Provision is made, of course, that substantially all the income received by the investment trust must be distributed to the shareholders.
With regard to investment trusts which have funded indebtedness the situation is slightly different.- In this case the corporation has issued fixed interest bearing securities to the public. The funds secured from the bondholders are then invested along with the funds received from the shareholders. It will be clear, I think, that any return obtained by the company in investing the funds received from the bondholders, in excess Of the fixed rate of interest paid to the bondholders, goes to the equity holders. In this sense, then, the corporation can be said to have made a profit for the equity holders in addition to having invested their funds advantageously. It seems therefore, that a half rate rather than full exemption would be fair and reasonable in the case of this kind of investment trust.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
This is complicated, and I believe I should make an. explanation. The effect of the legislation to be founded on this resolution is to offer an alternative method of determining the taxable portion of pensions received from funds, the income of which has been exempt from tax by reason of an election of the trustees of the fund. The section of the law which authorized this election was introduced in 1928 and was repealed in 1945.
During the period that a fund has been kept under this section, contributions made by the employee to the fund were not allowed as deductions from income, but the pension derived by the employee is subject to tax only in the proportion that contributions for which he was given deduction-that is, contributions made prior to 1928 or following 11945-bore to his total contribution to the fund. If all the contributions, for instance, were made between 1(928 and 1945, then the pension is totally exempt. Or, to take another example, if one-fifth of the contributions were made before 1928 and one-fifth after 1945, and the other three-fifths between 1928 and 1945, then two-fifths of the pension would be taxable and three-fifths of the pension would be tax exempt.
Representations have been made that this formula took no account of the portion of the final pension which arose from interest accumulations on the employee's contribution to the fund. If, for example, interest accumulations were added to the contributions made during the 1928 to 1945 period, the portion of the final pension actually attributable to these contributions would be larger, and the tax exempt proportion would be correspondingly increased. The effect of adding interest accumulation is mixed, however, depending upon the period in which the greater proportionate amount of the contributions were made.
If the greater part of the contributions were made before 1928, since these contributions determine the taxable proportion of the pension the accumulation of interest on these contributions would give less favourable treatment than that now provided in the law.
On the other (hand, if no contributions were made prior to 1928, a substantial proportion made in the period 1928 to 1945, and a lesser proportion made after 1945, the accumulation of interest would be more favourable than the present formula. Since the accumulation of interest is only of benefit under certain circumstances, it will be offered as an alternative which the taxpayer may take at his option.
The method now provided in law will be preserved, however, for pensioners who find it of greater benefit than the proposed alternative. In other words, this is another case Where an option is being given to the taxpayer to take one of two alternatives, whichever may be the more favourable.

The effect of the legislation to be based upon this resolution is to revise and make uniform the various provisions of the present law regarding the taxation of lump sum payments received from a superannuation or pension fund and from an employer on the occasion of retirement or loss of office. Under the existing law a lump sum payment from a superannuation or pension plan is taxable only to the extent of one-third, while lump sum payments on retirement or in respect of loss of office are taxable to the extent of one-fifth in the year of receipt and one-fifth in each of the following four years.
These provisions were introduced during the war to moderate the effect of very high tax rates when applied to a lump sum of money the whole of which is taxable income. In the case of payments out of a superannuation fund contributions to the fund would have been deductible when tax rates were much lower and the one-third rule had regard to this fact. In the meantime contributions have been deductible under high wartime tax rates, while lump sum payments out of the fund will be taxed at substantially reduced rates. It is proposed, therefore, to alter the provisions. All lump sum payments of the kind I have mentioned will be taxable at the option of the taxpayer either as income in the year of receipt or at a rate equal to the percentage which his total tax in the last full year of employment bears to his income in that year.
One alternative will be more favourable under certain circumstances than the other, depending upon the amount received in the
