speechtext:
That is provided for in section 3, subsection 8 of the Income War Tax Act which reads:
Where the minister is satisfied that a payment or payments made on or after the thirteenth day of October, nineteen hundred and forty-five by a person to a former employee is in respect of loss of office or employment, one-fifth only of the payment or the aggregate of the payments made in any year shall be deemed, for the purposes of this act, to be income of the taxpayer in the year it is received and one-fifth thereof shall be so deemed to be income of the taxpayer in each of the four succeeding years in which he is living.
That section is being amended by the legislation which will follow this resolution. As I indicated in my statement that was inserted in tire law at a time when the wartime rate of taxation were so high that it was felt that that was equitable under the circumstances.

I wonder why an arbitrary rule of that kind was resorted to. I think it would be more equitable to take the life expectancy of the individual and divide the payment into the number of years of expectancy. A man ceases to be employed and is paid a certain sum in lieu of salary for all time. If his expectancy were found to be ten years, why would it not be better to give him an income of one-tenth the total payment for each of the remaining ten years of his life? It seems to me that the present amendment will discourage payments to people who have rendered useful service. These payments will be considered to be futile because such a substantial portion will be going to the tax collector. Frequently it will make the income for the year greater than the taxpayer has ever earned during his earning years.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The proposed amendment will correct that. It was considered not only impracticable but most undesirable to take the life expectancy basis. Payments for loss of office cover men of a variety of ages, from the very young to the quite elderly, and they vary
Income War Tax

greatly in amount. A man who has a contract with an employer may have his contract terminated and be paid a certain sum of money as compensation. I do not think it would be proper to treat that as an annual payment to him for the rest of his life, based on his life expectancy. I think by and large the rule which was adopted under the section which I read of averaging it over five annual periods was about as close as one could come to a correct solution. Taking into account the fact that wartime rates of taxation were then high and that we are now coming into a period of reduced taxation, it is considered that the proposed rule provided for in this resolution is more equitable.

Would it not be better to wait until we get into the period of reduced taxation? I appreciate that there will be a reduction of sixteen per cent in income tax in 1946, but the tax is still a very burdensome one. It might easily mean that twenty-five or thirty per cent of the contribution which the employer wishes to make for the comfort and well-being of a faithful employee would go to the tax gatherer. It seems to me that that is unduly harsh, because in most cases the earning power of the individual has been terminated when these benefits accrue to him.
I take it that these payments in resolution 27 are in cases where a man on leaving gets one lump sum?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Right.

Of course, as the hon. member for Stanstead has pointed out, it is very unfortunate that the benefit should come in that way; it is not as good as a pension arrangement. Nothing is done, I take it, by way of anticipation to take care of the taxing situation such as is done in a pension plan. Is that true?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am advised that in a superannuation fund exemptions have been allowed to the taxpayer for the contributions he had made.

I come now to a matter of wording. The resolution says that the special provisions with regard to these payments shall:
... be replaced by a provision for the taxation of amounts so received after June 27, 1946, at the option of the taxpayer either as income for the year in which he received the amounts-
What amounts are those? We have been talking about one amount.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It probably should be in the singular. The resolution, as my hon. friend will notice, is drawn to cover three types of payments, payments out of a superannuation or pension fund, and payments by an employer to an employee upon retirement or loss of office, being payments of a lump sum but of a different nature. That may account for the use of the plural in the last paragraph. We shall be careful in the wording of the legislation.
The minister does not think we can successfully suggest that it is intended to refer to a series of amounts?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not think so.

We spent some time last year in fixing this at five years to overcome the effect of the option, and now we are going back to the same old provision as before. Could it be that the present provision has been taken advantage of, or what is the reason?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
This will not affect pending
cases.
I do not know whether there are any. I am wondering why, after changing to the five-year period, we are now going back to the earlier provision. We are reversing what we did last year.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We are entering on a period of reducing rather than increasing taxation.
That is an optimistic statement but hardly justifies this reduction from five years to one year. I am wondering if the existing clause has been taken advantage of to evade taxation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No.

Why is the administration not willing to accept what seems the most logical principle, namely, life expectancy? Or, if that it too complicated, why do they not give ten years or a stated number of years during which to write-off the gratuity or superannuation payment? We have had this matter up in previous years. It creates a great hardship when the whole amount is taxed in the year in which it is received. So that last year we made it five years, and I was hoping that now we would make it ten years. While there is an option in the proposed change, it seems to me that it will work a greater tax on the individual than the existing provision, which provides for a five-year spread of the capital payment. It is quite possible, indeed almost inevitable, that

Income War Tax
the tax on the capital sum at the rate of the man's last year of annual earnings will be at a great deal higher rate than the yearly spread over the next five years, and certainly over the next ten years. In other words, the man is retired and he has not much income in the great majority of cases that we are considering, and you are taxing him at higher rates than the ordinary individual who gets the same amount of money. When employers are trying to do the right thing by their employees by giving them a capital sum on leaving their service, the state should not step in and take away a little more than it takes from another individual who is getting the same amount of money. That is why I believe that life expectancy is the proper principle. If that is too complicated to work out, perhaps a ten-year period should be granted.

Why would it be too
complicated?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I do not take the stand
that it would be too complicated. I think it would be unfair to the general mass of taxpayers. Let me give an example. The employer gives his employee a lump sum on leaving his employ. The employer has no pension fund and so he gives his employee the equivalent, we will say, of six months' salary when he retires. $2,000 or $2,500 or something of that sort. That is a gratuity. It is income within the meaning of the act. But under the provisions of the existing law that could be spread over five years because the tax rates were then high. Under*the proposed amendment an option is given to the taxpayer. He can either take it as income for the year in which it is received and pay the tax on it at whatever the rates may be, or he may exclude it from his income if he has other income and have it taxed at a rate equal to the percentage which the tax upon the taxpayer's total income during his last full year of employment bore to his income in that year.

I understand quite well what the minister has said, but I am baffled a little by the basis he gives for his decision, that of fairness. I am sure it will be conceded that in the great majority of cases the man's usefulness as an earning and competitive entity is at an end. So why should we take any other basis for computing the gratuity than the number of years which he is going to live? He is getting that total amount in lieu of annual earnings for the rest of his life.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Not necessarily. These payments may have no particular relation to future earning power. His employer may retire him
at sixty. He is still active, and he retires with a lump sum because his employer does not have a pension fund. Then, being still active, he gets another position or earns money in other ways. His earning power is far from over. This provides that the payment does not have to be included in income for the year in which it is paid. I think that is fair. It may apply to any man from twenty-five to seventy-five years of age.

I admit that there may be exceptions, but cannot we agree that in most cases these lump sum payments are made to men who, in the appreciation of their employers, have reached the termination of their earning power? I am sure that if the minister goes over a very short category of his own acquaintances he will recall the names of many men who, while still active and in good health, cannot go out and get jobs. They were able to during the war because there was a great shortage of men. But the fact remains that in normal times the ordinary man whose services are dispensed with, whether it be by an insurance company, a brokerage house or an industrial concern, has reached the end of his competitive usefulness.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: A payment of this kind is not supposed to keep a man all his life. It is the equivalent of a few months' salary, a gratuity on retirement. It is not intended to keep him for the rest of his life; otherwise the equity as between different recipients would provide no connection at all. It would depend on age. A young man would have a big edge on the older man.

If he got $10,000 in one year and paid $3,500 income tax, and got
S10,000	gratuities, he would pay $3,500 on the same basis. Perhaps when we get an example we can understand it..

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Resolution agreed to.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that section 27 was carried at six o'clock. We might now revert to sections 18, 19 and 20, which were held in suspense.
18.	That for the 1946 and subsequent taxation years, the service pay and allowances, other than travelling allowances or separation allowances in place of travelling allowances, of a member of the permanent Canadian naval, military or air forces paid at the new rates of pay and allowances established for the said permanent forces be taxable income of a member irrespective of
Income War Tax

(a)	whether he is serving within or outside of Canada; or
(b)	whether he receives the pay and allowances during the first six months after his return to Canada.
19.	That for the 1917 and subsequent taxation years the pay and allowances of a member of the non-permanent Canadian naval, military or air forces other than the pay and allowances received by a member serving outside of the western hemisphere or within six months of his return thereto be taxable income of the said member and that the provisions for
(a)	a tax credit in respect of pay and allowances exceeding $1,600 as provided by rule 2 of section 3 of paragraph A of the first schedule; and for
(b)	taxation of a member serving outside of Canada in the western hemisphere at one-half the effective rate of tax applicable to his total income
be repealed.
20.	That the exemption of amounts received by members of the merchant marine as war risk bonuses in respect of service in a war risk zone and of the value of board and lodging received on shipboard, while performing service in respect of which such bonuses are payable be repealed for 1947 and subsequent taxation years.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I might make the usual
preliminary statement with reference to section 18 and the two following sections. These resolutions withdraw for the most part, from January 1, 1947, the special tax exemptions now granted members of the armed forces and the merchant marine. The present position regarding taxation of the armed forces may be summarized briefly as follows: 1. All personnel overseas are now entirely tax exempt. 2. Personnel in Canada are tax exempt on pay and allowance up to $1,600 a year if single and to higher amounts if married. As pay and allowances exceed these exempt amounts, they are made subject only gradually to the civilian tax rates through the operation of a diminishing tax credit. 3. Personnel in the western hemisphere but outside Canada pay only one-half the tax payable by forces stationed in Canada. 4. Pay and allowances of a member of the armed forces who returns from overseas and remains in the services are exempt for a period of six months. 5. Subsistence allowances up to $1.70 a day and travelling allowances are also exempt from tax under the present law.
The effect of the proposed change will be to make all permanent force personnel subject to ordinary income tax on their pay and allowances at the new permanent force rates, whe tllier in Canada or overseas, commencing from the inauguration of the new rates of pa}' in 1946, which will probably be somewhere about September or October. All other service personnel in Canada and in the western hemisphere outside Canada will be subject 
to full civilian tax from the beginning of 1947, while the overseas exemption will be continued only for the non-permanent force, a group rapidly diminishing in numbers. Exemption for six months after return to Canada will not be applicable to personnel receiving the new permanent force pay prior to their return to Canada, and tire exemption now given for subsistence allowance up to $1.70 a day will be repealed from the beginning of 1947. All other allowances paid under the new permanent force rates will be taxable income with the exception of separation allowances paid in place of travelling allowances. The latter are now exempt under the law and will continue to be exempt. In keeping with this revision of the income tax as it applies to the armed services, resolution 20 provides for repeal, effective in 1947, of the special exemption granted the merchant marine in respect of war risk bonus and the value of board and lodging.

May I ask two questions in
connection with that statement? Am I to understand that from the time the permanent rates of pay come into effect there will be no such thing as income tax exemption for any of the men in the permanent force?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
In respect of these rates of pay; that is correct.
Mr. GREE'N: What about the men who will not be in the permanent force but will still be on service? Are they to lose the exemptions they have at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The position there wilL be this. All the overseas personnel other than the permanent force will continue to enjoy the exemption which is now granted them under the law. In other words, we shall observe our contract in that respect. Interim force personnel who are over there were given an assurance when they joined the interim force that there would be no change in their tax status during the two-year period, which will expire September 30, 1947. That will be respected. In the case of men who apply for entry into the permanent force and are accepted for that force, and who receive the new rates of pay provided for that force, they are looked upon as having entered a permanent post-war career and should be subject to the ordinary rules with respect to the payment of tax. Broadly speaking, it was felt that from January 1, 1947, the special wartime exemptions from income tax for overseas service, or qualified exemption for service in Canada, should be discontinued, and it should be considered that from that day on. those serving in the armed forces

Income War Tax
would be serving like those in other occupations and there should be no special income tax exemptions.

Apparently there will be some serving in Canada and elsewhere, in the western hemisphere, after the first of January.
In other words, for them war service has not yet ended. Why deprive them of their present exemption? I presume they will be all out of the forces by the end of 1947. Why should that exemption not carry on while they are in the forces? They are required. apparently, to perform certain duties in connection with the cleaning up of the aftermath of war. W hy not continue to them the exemption they now enjoy?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not contemplate that after January 1, 1947 there will be anyone in the forces, either in Canada or overseas, who is not a member of either the permanent force or the interim force. If there are such persons overseas they will continue to enjoy the income tax exemption which is now provided. whether they are interim force or hostilities-only personnel. Should there be cases of hostilities-only personnel who are still retained in the service after January 1, 1947-
In Canada or in the western hemisphere?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There are none except in Canada now; we have them away from all other parts of the western hemisphere. Under the legislation as it is proposed, they would lose the qualified income tax exemption which now exists. But I frankly do not anticipate that there will be any of that class. If there are, and there is any hardship, we shall be prepared to consider it on a special basis, but I do not anticipate that there will be any in the armed forces after January 1, 1947, who will be deprived of any benefit they now enjoy. The position will be preserved for those who enlisted in the interim: force on the understanding that their tax position would not be changed during the period of enlistment and who had the option of serving for that period, or of applying to go into the permanent force.
Perhaps when the minister is going over the bill he will insert something to protect the men who enlisted, who are on what is called hostilities service; is that it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Hostilities-only. I use that phrase because it is convenient.

Hostilities-only service. The minister says now that he does not think there will be any of them, and therefore there
will not be any tax. But just in case there are some I suggest that the section be drawn accordingly.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall be glad to give consideration to that when the bill comes before the house. I can point out that rare cases of that kind can be dealt with by remissions under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, but I shall give consideration to my hon. friend's point.

Has any consideration
been given to the policy in the future in the event that Canadian forces should be serving outside Canada. For example, if Canada is required to supply some units of the air force or of the army under agreement with the united nations and they have to go abroad either across the Atlantic or across the Pacific, is it the policy of the government that they will receive no consideration by way of tax exemptions?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I can give my hon. friend onlv my personal opinion. No consideration has been given to the matter by the government, but my personal opinion is this, and it has always been this, that there should be no special income tax exemption for those serving in the armed forces. There is none in the British force. This is only my own personal opinion, but I believe that there should be no income tax exemptions for those serving in the armed forces.

Is the minister against
granting income tax exemptions such as those that were granted in the last war?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I had no opportunity of exercising any views in regard to the exemptions, but since my hon. friend has asked me the question directly I would say, yes. I believe that the system which is followed in the British army is correct, and 'that there should be no special income tax exemption.	I grant that every consideration
should be given to those in the armed forces, but it should be by means of the .pay scale and not by income tax exemption. That is my personal belief. Since my hon. friend has asked me the question as to what the policy will be in the future, I must say that I cannot say what it will be, but in so far as my own views would have any weight I would urge that the British system be followed and that we not have an income tax exemption.

There is one other question that I should like to raise on this resolution, namely, the taxation of men in the auxiliary services and the corps of fire-fighters who served during the war. Probably some of them are still serving. On the 23rd of July
Income War Tax

a recommendation was made to the house by the special committee on veterans affairs which reads as follows:
That the supervisors of the auxiliary services and fire-fighters of the corps of Canadian Fire Fighters dispatched overseas, and members of the Canadian Red Cross Society and the St. John ambulance brigade who served in an actual theatre of war. be accorded all benefits, pensions, rehabilitation rights and income tax exemption as members of the armed forces.
Unfortunately the men of the auxiliary services and perhaps the men of the fire-fighters- I am not sure what percentage 'they were exempt, but in any event the men of the auxiliary services were allowed only a one-fifth exemption.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is correct.

In previous years we pointed out to the government the ihequity of the arrangement, and I suggest that this is the time to remedy the situation. The income tax payments which have been taken from these men should be refunded to them. As an example, take the men in the auxiliary services. They included the men in the legion war services-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The Y.M.C.A.

The Knights of Columbus, the Y.M.C.A., and the Salvation Army. The men from these forces served with the troops. In Hong Kong the only two men in the whole force who had to pay income tax were the Y.M.C.A. man and the Knights of Columbus man. They came back to Canada and found that they owed the government several hundred dollars. I think it ran over 81,000 or perhaps into the thousands for income tax-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: They must have had a big income.

-and these amounts were taken from them. That situation is unfair. Other men serving under fire with the troops in Italy had to pay income tax. They were allowed only one-fifth exemption. This matter was thoroughly discussed in the veterans affairs committee. Evidence was given there which, I think, clinches the matter. I would refer hon. members to page 206 of the committee proceedings.
Order.

These proceedings have been reported back to the house. General Bums, who is in charge of rehabilitation, was a corps commander in Italy. In the committee he said:

We have Colonel Philpott here to-day. He was deputy director of auxiliary services for the Canadian army overseas, and he could possibly answer the question for you.
The question asked was as to the status of those men of the auxiliary service. Colonel Philpott was then called on, and said:
Mr. Chairman, I think the answer you are trying to get is this: first of all the supervisor, in my opinion, was definitely a member of the forces. His services, and the conditions under which he served, were exactly the same as those of other members of the forces.
Then at page 207 the chairman said:
With regard to one point you mentioned. I agree with what you say in a large measure that to most intents and purposes these supervisors were members of the armed services, but they could not be ordered into combat or anything like that?
Colonel Philpott:	They were non-combatants,
but they were right up with the troops in the fighting. They were looking after our troops' welfare right in the front line. I can vouch for them because it was my job to direct them. I was with them on the continent and I was with them with the troops, and they suffered the same hardships and privations and had the same discipline.
I could go on at considerable length, but there is the whole story. I am not going to try to pile any further arguments on top of the statement that was made by Colonel Philpott who was actually in the government service.
With regard to the corps of fire-fighters, hon. members will bear in mind that, at the time these men were recruited, fire-fighting in Great Britain was considered even more dangerous than being in the forces. That was at the time when the Germans were bombing English cities. These men were enlisted to undergo these hardships and they actually did so. Further than that, we had an affidavit produced before us in the committee, sworn to by thirty-eight members of this corps of fire-fighters, which reads as follows:
We, the undersigned, hereby jointly and severally swear that we were present at'Parliament hill. Ottawa, on the occasions when Major-General LaFleche, deputy minister of national war services, made statements to contingents of the corps of Canadian fire-fighters, on their leaving for overseas, as follows:
He stated that we would be looked after in the same manner as the armed forces, that our families would receive the same protection and benefits that were accorded the army, and that we were to be known as the fourth arm of the services. (A term that the governor general used while addressing us.)
This affidavit will be found at page 317 of the proceedings of the committee. Evidence was given by Mr. Magill, one of the executives of their association, who was asked this question by the hon. member for Lanark:
Yes, what were your services?

Income War Tax
The answer was:
When we volunteered for this job, we did not ask any questions as to what we were going to get or what we were not going to get. We volunteered to go over, and when we joined the corps we knew that we were going over; in two months, every man from the time he enlisted, was overseas. When we got there we were attached to the national fire service. The membership of the national fire service was obtained on a compulsory basis.
That was in Great Britain.
The men in England could either go into the army, navy, the air force, or the fire service. They had no option. It was considered a branch of the services there. When we got there we were attached to the national fire service. They in turn gave us vital points to protect from fire. We went to Southampton, Portsmouth, Plymouth and Bristol. Those cities were receiving at that time the greatest brunt of the bombing. We worked in conjunction with them all through. We maintained our own station, with our own officers and our own men, equipment supplied by the national fire service. We were trained over there by them and attended their colleges and also took courses over there with them.
Then he was asked:
Go ahead. Tell us what you actually did; for instance when there was an air raid, what did you do?
One of the other members asked:
Was not a detachment ready to go to France on D-day?
The answer was yes; then the witness went on:
In the event of a raid we immediately went outside in the street and took up our positions at our stations. We could not take cover. Our job was outside, not inside, when the raid was on. We had to stand outside. A station would perhaps have five or six pumps in it. Immediately on the warning being given they would be dispersed to certain points in the city and the men would have to stand there until they received instructions where the raid was and what they were to do. There was no chance for us to take cover.
Then the hon. member for Lanark asked:
Q. In the event of a fire during the raid, what did you do?
A. During the raid we immediately went to the fire.
Q. In spite of the fact that bombs might be falling?
A. It did not make any difference. We answered the call.
Q. You would -work practically all through a raid?
A. Yes, outside. That was our job. We did have 100 men trained and attached to the 21st army group ready to leave for France on D-day, and they got on the boat. They actually took their training and got on the landing barges, and then were taken off. We trained for that and had army personnel attached to us in a liaison capacity, so that when we went over there we knew where we were going and what we were going to do. But fortunately, the raids in France did not develop to anything like what was expected. Therefore we were not needed. But we were prepared to leave and ready to leave at a moment's notice.
Several of these men were killed; others were seriously wounded and others were injured, and I do suggest to the acting finance minister that before the bill based upon this resolution is brought down consideration should be given to providing exemption from income tax for these groups for whom the committee has put in a recommendation. All these questions have been carefully considered by the veterans affairs committee, and its recommendations should be given great weight. I do not think anyone can question the justice of the claims of these particular groups.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Perhaps I might deal at once with some of the points raised by my hon. friend. I am thoroughly familiar with the questions he has brought forward; I lived with them for four or five months when I was parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance. Under the law as it stands, complete income tax exemption has been granted only to those who were members of the armed forces; and the policy has consistently been that it was not considered appropriate to grant complete income tax exemption to civilian groups, no matter what the risk involved in the particular work they were doing.
To give the committee an idea of the civilian groups involved, there are the auxiliary services, to which my hon. friend has referred, such as the Knights of Columbus, the Y.M.C.A. and the like; the fire-fighters, to which he has also referred; those who served in the merchant marine; the pilots who served in the ferry command; the test pilots and the civilian instructors in the flying schools. All these groups have claimed income tax exemption. The policy has been consistently that complete income tax exemption should be granted only to those serving in the armed forces. May I interject here that this illustrates, if I may say so, the desirability of not granting complete income tax exemption to any group in the community, because it leads to more or less well founded claims by other groups who feel that they have an equal right to exemption?
Take the case of the auxiliary services. For reasons which no doubt were well founded, the members of these services preferred to serve under the auspices of their various organizations rather than as members of the armed services.
That story was gone into by the committee, and the facts are just the opposite.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: If my hon. friend will permit me to finish what I have to say-

But the minister must not make an incorrect statement.

Income War Tax

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
My hon. friend had his turn, and I did not interrupt him. I met a committee of the auxiliary services two years ago and discussed this question of tax exemption for the auxiliary services. In that committee I raised this point, and discussed it at length with them. It was agreed by the members of that committee that this was the case; that, not necessarily for reasons of their own, I do not suggest, but for good and sufficient reasons they preferred to serve under their own auspices. In the United States army by contrast, the auxiliary services were provided by the armed forces themselves. The men who served in them were army personnel, subject to army discipline, receiving army rates of pay and so on.
The auxiliary services are in law civilians, and they were such because their organizations so desired. The same thing applies, of course, to the merchant marine, ferry command pilots, test pilots and civilian instructors. It was felt that in the case of these groups some income tax consideration should be given; and in the case of the auxiliary services, after the discussion with this committee to which I have refer-, red, legislation was introduced by order in council granting an exemption of one-fifth of the supervisor's pay, which was treated as exempt from income tax. That was roughly comparable to the treatment accorded merchant seamen, where their war risk bonus was considered as exempt from income tax. In the case of the ferry command, if I remember correctly, it was one-third. There, of course, the scale of remuneration was fairly high, and that was looked upon as the war risk element of their pay. Offhand I cannot remember what was done, if anything, in the case of test pilots or civilian instructors; but I am advised that it is now under consideration, if it is not already passed, that the fire-lighters will receive treatment similar to that accorded the auxiliary services and the merchant seamen.
What rate is that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: In the case of the merchant seamen it was the war risk bonus, and in the case of the auxiliary services it was one-fifth of the pay, which would be roughly comparable for those categories. In addition, these groups have been given the further benefits, pension benefits and the like, accorded to members of the armed forces.
No, not yet.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That has been recommended, and I believe it is to be done. However, the point I want to emphasize here is that the principle has never been recognized that any civilian group in Canada will be-granted complete income tax exemption.

That has been considered a fundamental principle of government policy, and it is one, I may say, to which I thoroughly subscribe, in the light of the views I have expressed in respect to income tax exemptions to any groups generally.
Broadly speaking, that is the position with respect to these various civilian groups. I want the committee to understand that I do not wish in any way to be considered as casting any reflection on the value of the services performed by these groups or the risks which may have been involved in performing those services. On the contrary, I have only the greatest admiration for the work they performed; but I say we cannot recognize the principle that any civilian group is to be completely exempt from income tax.

There is just one thing I
want to say in that connection in regard to the point on which the minister's whole argument is based. He says that these men had this status at their own request. The evidence before the committee was just the opposite, namely that the status they had was at the insistence of the army.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am in a position-

The minister did not want
me to interrupt him. Let him just sit down until I have finished. The army insisted that while they were in-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Who gave that evidence?

Different people gave it, and it was not questioned by the army authorities. It was the army that made them serve in the way that they did. In the first war they carried rank badges; in this last war they did the same -work but there was a ruling by the army that they must be treated in the way that they were treated-not, strictly speaking, considered as members of the army. They are now deprived of income tax exemption, although many of them were actually under fire, and yet others who were never under fire are getting it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I was not at the meeting of the veterans committee to which the hon. member referred, but I was present at a meeting at national defence headquarters two years ago which was presided over by Brigadier Mess, and at which were present senior representatives of the auxiliary services. Representatives of all these services were there, including my friend Jack Beaton of the Y.M.C.A.
The question was raised at that time as to what the status of the auxiliary services was, and we had a considerable discussion on that

Income War Tax
matter. The point was clearly brought out, and it was brought out by Brigadier Mess and brought out by myself, that the condition under which they were serving was not because the army wished it that way but because the auxiliary services wished it that way.
I was not present at the veterans affairs committee; but I know what was said at the meeting two years ago; I know who the representatives were, and I know who presided at the meeting.
Does Jack Beaton know?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: He will, because he was in on that meeting and he will recall what took place. There was one other meeting.
You ask him.

Further to what the hon. member for Vancouver South had to say about Canadian overseas fire-fighters, I wish to reiterate what he said about promises that were made to the corps before proceeding overseas. They were promised definitely by Major-General LaFleche, as representative of the government at that time, that they would receive all privileges which would be granted to the armed services.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext:
Would you permit a
question?

When I am through you can make your speech.
Mr. -ABBOTT: May he put a question-

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: Yes, may I put a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: What is your foundation for your statement that General LaFleche made a promise to the auxiliary services?
I read the affidavit a minute ago.
There is the sworn statement- as to the overseas fire-fighters.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: I challenge that.

Well, that will be your responsibility. But the affidavit was made to say definitely that the Canadian overseas firefighters would be given the privilege of having income tax exemptions. It was only after they came back that they received notice of this back income tax which they were forced to pay. But I should like to ask the minister, who is responsible for not taxing these overseas fire-fighters at the source? It was done in every other case where there was a payment of income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I cannot say why they were not, but I will look into that situation.
Would the Minister of National Revenue answer that?

I wish to support as strongly as I can the remarks imade by my deskmate, the hon. member for Vancouver South, particularly those remarks in regard to the fire-fighters, because I am more familiar with their case than with other cases of the other services mentioned. I knew quite a number of fire-fighters who left Toronto. Several of the leading members of the overseas brigade came from my riding, and I have learned from them and have had communications from their association in Toronto outlining what they went through.
If, as my colleague has pointed out, they were made promises-and that I do not know, but I listened to the affidavit read by my colleague-I am sure the minister and certainly all hon. members in the house would want that agreement carried out-. A number were killed and a number badly injured. They went into action when the buzz bombs were at their worst. They were in the thick of what took place which, at times, was as bad as anything that took place on the continent itself. So I just wish to add my support to what has been said as to relieving them from what has been imposed upon them.

While we are on this question, I would point out that the minister said it was a matter of policy not to grant complete tax exemption to any other than those who served in the armed forces. Then he went on to say that certain groups did receive consideration and that claims of other groups were put forward at a meeting at which he was present.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The meeting to which I referred was the auxiliary services only.

The question I would ask him is whether or not consideration has been given, or whether representatives have been made on behalf of a small group of Canadians, only twelve or fourteen in number, who served with the Canadian forces from Sicily through to Germany, on whose behalf, so far as I know, no benefits have been extended. I refer to the Canadian war correspondents. Has any application been made or any consideration given to income tax relief for them during that period?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I am advised that certain representations were made to the Minister of Finance on behalf of certain war correspondents, but I am not in a position to give any more particulars than that at the present time.
Income War Tax
I am informed that they are some twelve or fourteen in number, and I believe the total amount involved would be less than $10,000.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: May I point out that this, again, just bears out my point. I am not so much interested in the amount of money involved, but I am arguing strongly the question of principle, that if you extend this exemption to one civilian group, then I can think of a lot more to whom I think it might with equal justice be extended.

I am not going to add to the minister's list extensively. But I say that whether or not you accept the minister's idea, that in principle it is wrong, the practice was accepted. Perhaps the time to change a principle is between wars, not during one or at the end of one. Perhaps when the minister is considering these applications he would look into this small group.

Before we leave the question of fire-fighters, I should like to say that I shall be glad to supply the Minister of National Revenue with proof that this promise was made to them by a minister of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: He was deputy minister, was he not?
I shall be glad to supply it to you; I have it in my file.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think he was deputy minister at the time.

Deputy minister. While the Acting Minister of Finance refers to the principle, I feel that here is one place where the opposition is truly trying to help out the government with its principles. A promise was made to these men and there are signed statements in witness of that promise being made. I know it is with great regret that many of therm have brought the matter into public affairs to-day. I feel that if any group should receive consideration it is this particular group because a promise was made to them.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not know7 whether a promise was made or not; but, assuming for the sake of argument that it was, I would point out that no civil servant, no matter what position he occupied, would have any authority to make such a promise. That would be contrary to the income tax law as it stands.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think I said that was under consideration. I do not know that I am in position to make a statement.

The minister is not prepared to go even that far. If I were to enter into a debate as to whether or not these firefighters should receive the same privileges as the men who served in uniform I would need to mention only one statement made by the minister, shall I say in his proper capacity as Minister of National Defence, and I am not saying that he cannot handle the position

Income War Tax
he is now in quite efficiently. But he did make this statement, and very heatedly as I remember, one day in reply to a member of the official opposition. He said that so far as he was concerned, wherever the bombs were falling, whether it be in England or any place else, that was the front line.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not remember making such a statement, although I may have. It does not sound like my type of oratory, but it may be correct.

I shall not cite any of the promises or anything of that kind, but I think I can meet the minister on his own terms of high principle. I like the minister for advancing the idea that we should deal with these matters on terms of high principle.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Principle, anyway.

I like his idea that there should be general taxation and relief by means of higher pay to the armed forces. We must deal with this matter on practical terms and not in terms of the future. The high principle the minister speaks of is that advanced by this government that no civilian group which served overseas shall have the same exemption from taxation as was granted to the members of the armed forces.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Not necessarily overseas; no civilian group anywhere.

I agree with that high principle; but let. me say that in the case of the auxiliary services and the fire-fighters the acting minister, unwittingly I am sure, is descending from that high principle to a verbal technicality in the way he is applying it to these two classes. Evidence has been given by the member for Vancouver South that a statement was made by the officer responsible for administering the auxiliary services to the effect that they were undistinguishable from soldiers in their service, in the discipline that was imposed on them, in the places they had to go and in the various duties they carried out. Technically and because of mere verbiage, these mem are treated as civilians when in actual fact they were just as much soldiers as any one in the forces. The auxiliary services are in a class by themselves.
The fire-fighters were serving in England and they were considered as being on all fours with the armed forces. I remember speaking to one man who was called up, and he told me that he had been permitted to elect between the army and the fire-fighters when he received his call-up. They were
just as glad to get fire-fighters as they were to get soldiers. The military need for that class of men was just as great as it was for soldiers, and they were glad to have these men go over at a time when, goodness knows, soldiers were needed. That is absolute proof to my mind that in high principle they were soldiers, and it is only begging the point to say that they were not.

Following what the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard has said in connection with the fire-fighters, I would point out that they received the same rates of pay as those in the armed forces. In answer to the Minister of National Revenue I would say that these fire-fighters proceeded overseas in detachments of fifty or so. The promise was made by Major-General LaFleche to each detachment in the same terms; it was not made on only one occasion; it was made on several occasions. They were told that they would receive the same consideration as those in the armed forces.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext:
The only reason I asked
the hon. gentleman a question was to find out whether that assurance had been made verbally or in writing. This matter came before me as Minister of National War Services. I had the officers of the department make a complete search, and I made one personally, of all the records and correspondence, and nowhere could we find that a commitment had been made to the fire-fighters with reference to exemption from income tax.
The hon. member for Vancouver South brought up a point with reference to pay, that it should be such that the paying of income tax would not be a hardship. The chief of the fire-fighting services was receiving in his occupation in this country before he left for overseas $2,400 a year, and as chief of the fire-fighting services he received, a salary of $5,000 a year, so that in that instance at least the rate of pay was such that he could, I think, have met the requirements which my hon. friend says should be met with reference to pay.
What about the firemen?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext:
I think the hon. member for Wentworth is correct when he says that their rates of pay were the same as in the armed services. I am not detracting one iota from the service this force rendered. I am merely asking anyone to indicate to me if he can that there was any assurance to the fire-fighters they would be exempt from income tax?
Income War Tax

Certainly it was a verbal promise, and given on more than one occasion. But it was never denied by any member of the government, and the fire-fighters were most certainly led to believe that they would receive all the privileges of the armed services. I said in this house in 1937, I think it was, when the estimates of the Department of Pensions and National Health were up for discussion, that every government since the last great war had chiseled on the returned men, and I meant every government, both Liberal and Conservative. .

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: This one has not. It is giving the returned men the most generous deal of any country in the world.
I am speaking of 1937. But most certainly this government is not living up to its obligations in regard to the fire-fighters.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am not prepared to concede that this government entered into any obligation to the fire-fighters with respect to income tax. I have made that clear already, but I must reiterate it in view of my hon. friend's statement.
It would be interesting to know if the Minister of National Revenue ever went to General LaFleche and asked him if he ever made that promise.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: When the matter came before me personally, General LaFleche had left the country to serve as ambassador to Greece. What my hon. friend asks was done, and General LaFleche could not recall having made any commitment.
Did he deny that he made it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: He did not recall having made any commitment.
But he did not deny it?

Regarding the supervisors of the auxilary services, in world war I, they wore the rank and were recognized as being in the army. I also have attended conferences. The Minister of National Defence, who is conducting this legislation through the committee, mentioned having attended a conference in 1942, where he said-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: About 1943 or 1944.

It is immaterial. He attended a conference where he said that the heads of the organization at that time expressed a desire that their personnel should remain as civilians and not be incorporated in the army.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I know that my hon. friend wants to be correct. They acknowledged at that meeting that the status which the auxiliary services occupied as civilians under their own control and direction was at their own desire and request and not at the request of the armed forces.

At their own desire and request. I should like to say that I have also attended conferences. I attended conferences in 1939 on board a ship going over to England, and I know the commander of the first Canadian division at that time was firm in his opinion that he did not want the auxiliary services as part of the army. I think that should be on the record in order that hon. members may see that the army as well as the organizations were not anxious that the personnel should be considered part of the army.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It may have been mutual. I do not deny that.

I should like to point this out, that there was an interchange between the army and these services. Sometimes an individual was in the auxiliary services and later was transferred into the army, and vice versa, some of the personnel who were in the army were at times transferred into the auxiliary services. During 1939, 1940 and 1941 there were staff officers on the headquarters of formations whose special duty it was to supervise the supervisors of the auxiliary services. They were with the headquarters of formations, while the supervisors themselves were with the units. Those officers would be exempt from income tax, whereas the supervisors who were in the more advanced units were not exempt. It does not seem to me to add up and be fair that you should give one class of men exemption when another class of men doing exactly similar work were not exempt.

Just one further word, and I am compelled to say it because of the remark made by the Minister of National Revenue that the fire-fighters were paid merely the same rate of pay as a private in the army. Of course, the majority of the firefighters overseas would be in the lower ranks. I am personally acquainted with many of them who were in the Toronto fire department, where they received the Toronto fire department remuneration. Quite a number of them were lieutenants or of higher rank when serving with the Toronto fire department, but they took a lower rank in the fire-fighting service overseas because of their patriotic desire to serve their country "over there". I know that in a number of cases while they

Income War Tax
were overseas their wives and families had a struggle to get along. I did not know before that their pay while overseas was so low. In view of that low pay, I should like to see the government give them any consideration which cam be given. It does seem to me that five per cent is a pretty small allowance. I hope the Acting Minister of Finance will reconsider their case. He shakes his head. He is pretty determined, and I have no fault to find with that because I like to see a man stick up for his opinions. But I would urge him to give consideration to the strong recommendation which has been made by the hon. member for Vancouver South, who is always on the job when anything pertaining to the armed forces or the auxiliary services comes up. I hope the minister will reconsider the case of the fire-fighters.

This question has -been covered fairly extensively, but I want to bring one point to the attention of the minister. These men who had been given this promise by General LaFleche could not have just imagined that they had been given this promise. Groups of these men have come to see me from various parts of Canada, and each of them have told me individually and collectively that they had received a definite and specific promise, verbally I grant you, that they would be exempted from income tax. It seems to me that if we are talking about high principles, the verbal assurance of a minister of the crown-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I must correct that. He was not a minister of the crown at the time.
Well, a deputy minister of the crown and subsequently a minister.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Right.

I say that his verbal assurance, his word, should be as good as his bond. Many of these men have come to me and said, "We joined the fire-fighters because, had we joined the army and declared our occupation, we would immediately have been sent to some fire-fighting unit and put on fire-fighting duty at some permanent camp in Canada." I know that is what happened, because trained firemen, like other trained persons were at a high premium during the war, and many of these men definitely joined the fire-fighters because that was their only opportunity to get overseas. They feel, and is it a justifiable feeling on their part, that they are being badly treated, scandalously treated, because certainly in their own minds, there is the belief that a promise was given them by General LaFleche.
They also feel another grievance. It has nothing directly to do with this question, but the minister is also Minister of National Defence and he should know about it. I understand that they did not get the service decorations that the armed personnel were given, the reason being that they were civilians. Here we have the case of a man who joined the armed forces, who perhaps was a member of a fire brigade, who went to Cam-p Borden and did duty there as a firefighter. He is in his unit as a fire-fighter and gets three decorations or two perhaps, whereas the fellow that went overseas and actually put out incendiary fires has no decorations- has he? An hon. member says he has. I understand that was one of their grievances, but perhaps that has been corrected.
At any rate, in the m-atter of income tax, these men were unquestionably given an assurance, even though perhaps it cannot be found on the minister's files. There were only a few of these men. Surely, from the principle that we have heard enunciated, the high principle that the government should make its deputy minister's word as good as its own, the minister should take the representations of these men into consideration. It is not a m-atter involving a great amount of money; it is not a matter of extravagance; it is a matter of simple justice. I ask, therefore, that this case be reconsidered, in the hope that these men will receive the benefit that was at least verbally promised them. There is in another room in this building a committee which has twice recommended that.

I support the views expressed by the hon. member who has just spoken. I suppose that the minister and also the Minister of National Revenue mean what they say when they assert that no commitment was given, or that General LaFleche cannot recall having made a promise. I have talked to some of these men who were fire-fighters. They do not lie in other matters and they honestly believe that the promise was made. Many of them have signed their names to a document to the effect that it is their conviction that the promise in question was given, and others are prepared to sign their names to the same thing. In other words, they went into this particular service on the strength of their belief that the promise was made. What earthly principle can- now be invoked for denying to these men the fulfilment of that promise, to which they are willing to swear in an affidavit, because the assurance was given by a government official? This must have been known to the cabinet ministers at the time.
Income War Tax

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It was not.
The minister says it was not and I shall have to take his word for that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am only saying that on hearsay.

But when so many people in the country fully believe that the promise was made and when so many of these men have themselves told me that they believed the promise was given, the cabinet must have known about it. Nearly everyone who follows the papers in the country knows it. It is not something that has just recently come up. If I have heard the discussion rightly to-night, both ministers who spoke said that there were no deductions from the payments to the firefighters overseas. Well, how does the Department of National Revenue propose to collect now from those from whom collections were not made at the source? Is the department going to go into the courts and sue these people and take their knives and forks and their frying-pans from them? How will they get the money if they have not collected it? In view of the belief that these men entertain, that the promise was made, what high principle can be invoked to afford the government any excuse to take the attitude which the minister is taking?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Fairness as between classes of taxpayers. It is perfectly clear, I am assured by the officials, that there was never any agreement on the part of the responsible minister, the Minister of Finance, that such an exemption would be given. I am not denying that these men may have believed that they were to receive income tax exemption; but if they are to receive it, then there are a number of other groups who have an equal if not a greater claim. These men performed a most useful service under great risks. The casualties were two out of four hundred odd-I am only told that. But let us assume-
I believe three were killed and others were wounded.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That may be so. In any event, there were about one-third of the ferry pilots lost. If this treatment were extended to the fire-fighters, a civilian group, in my opinion it would have to be extended to the ferry pilots and other equally deserving groups. I can only reiterate what I have previously said, that no civilian as such has been recognized as being entitled to complete income tax exemption, and no responsible minister of the crown ever gave an undertaking that they would be. I do not think that principle can now be recognized.
I still do not believe the minister is taking the right attitude.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is a matter of opinion.

I believe there are other civilians who have as good a claim or perhaps better, but no other civilian group who engaged in any type of war service comparable with that of the fire-fighters believe that they were given such a promise. They were not brought into the service in which they were engaged under any promise of the kind. But these people believe that they were given that promise, because it was given by a high government official who enjoyed considerable popularity in the country. If any other group came forward with similar evidence and the same conviction on their part of a promise that had been made to them to join a certain service, I would say that they had as much right to consideration. But this was distinctly the understanding that these men had.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I cannot believe that these men joined the service because they thought they would get income tax exemption.
Certainly not, but that does not say that they were not given the promise.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I suggest that, whether or not the undertaking was given on that point, which seems to be debated across the floor, the matter should be settled on the basis of the principle which the minister himself has stated, namely, fairness as between taxpayers. The argument that if these people are entitled to this exemption others would have to be considered as well is not an argument against these people being given it. That might only mean the others should receive it as well. In that connection, I felt that the Minister of National Revenue got away from the point when he referred to one of the members of the corps of fire-fighters receiving greater pay for his services in the corps than his remuneration in civil life. The hon. member for Vancouver South suggests that was only one case out of hundreds so far as fire-fighters are concerned; but the point I wish to make is that is not a proper comparison to make. If one is to make that comparison it will certainly upset a good many calculations so far as the armed services are concerned. The comparison should be with similar war service. On that basis, I suggest that these men should be treated in a manner similar to that of those in the armed services.
The very fact that there are items Nos. 7 and 8 on the order paper under government orders, to which I believe the minister has already referred, represents to me an admia-

Income War Tax
sion that these men have been discriminated against unfairly and that certain wrongs must be righted. The fact that these other wrongs have to be righted lends strength to our argument that this wrong should be righted as well.	[DOT]
I should like to bring to the attention of the minister one other point which relates to the effort in which some of us were engaged for a considerable period with reference to the Canadian soldiers who went to Kiska. When they went the income tax regulations did not recognize the fact that Kiska was outside the western hemisphere, and they were taxed at once and paid the tax through deductions at the source as though they were serving within the western hemisphere. After considerable effort on the part of some of us in the house, the government, by order in council, changed the regulations. That was some months after the deductions had been made, but once the justice of the claim had been recognized it was found possible to make the change retroactive. I am sorry to say it took the department a long time to take care of the matter, but at any rate, the justice of the principle being recognized later with respect to these men and retroactive action being taken, I submit that it should also be done in this case.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That was due, I take it, to a mistaken understanding of facts. These men were in the army; they were soldiers, and at that time it was merely a question of where they were serving.
There is one other thing I should like to say with respect to these fire-fighters. It has been brought to my attention that this alleged promise was given as the men were leaving for overseas. None of them alleged that it was given at the time they joined.

Speaking as a civilian from a soldier city, I wish the government under resolution 18 would give these men who were combatant soldiers, who served overseas in different theatres of the war, at least three years to reestablish themselves before starting in to tax them. The government should start in on some of the higher-ups before taxing soldiers so soon. Judging by the way the security councils are blowing up in Europe, I can tell the committee that we shall not have security for very long, and we may need these men a little later on. I believe that the money could be provided in some other way and that we should wait for at least three years before we start taxing soldiers who were at the front.

I do not wish to repeat
the arguments which have been used. This matter was discussed in the veterans committee for a good many hours and almost all points were brought out. While these men were not recruited as soldiers, they were recruited to do practically soldier's work. They were assigned difficult and dangerous tasks. At the time they enlisted and after enlistment they were treated practically as soldiers; they were under the same as military discipline all the time that they were away. Their pay was practically the same as the soldier's pay, if not the same. As far as their duties were concerned, in England we all know that for the first two years of the war the soldiers who were overseas had very little to do except training. These men were looking after fires in all the devastated areas in England. Anyone who has been to London and the different cities and has seen the destruction in those cities realizes the dangers which these men have gone through and will realize that their work was practically the same as the work that was carried on by soldiers in France.
I should also like to point out to the minister that many thousands of men who were recruited and acted as soldiers got this exemption. These men were on the staffs in England. They spent all their time in England doing necessary work so far as the army was concerned, but so far as the dangers they encountered are concerned as compared with the dangers encountered by these men, there was no comparison at all.
I understood that these men were asked to go to England after the Prime Minister had been to that country and had seen the devastation there. He came back and realized that it was necessary that we send some of the men over. There was also a request from the British government. From personal interview with some of these men, I know it was their intention to join the armed forces and go overseas; but they were told that they could do better work if they went over as fire-fighters and assisted in the putting out of fires, and helped in the devastated area of the different cities. It is not necessary to press this point any farther.
So far as the justice of the claim is concerned, it was recognized in our veterans committee that these men should receive consideration. There were less than three hundred of them-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Four hundred.

I think 378 or something like that. In any event, the number is not large. It would be only a matter of justice if the minister and the government would reconsider the attitude they have taken and
Income War Tax

exempt these men from income tax. They were away from their families just as the soldiers were.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There were a number of civilians in London who rendered devoted service on the same basis.

Who were they? The
minister has already mentioned the pilots. Our committee recommended that these pilots should receive consideration. They are receiving some consideration but they are not getting exemption in taxes. One of the arguments used in our committee was that these men received much larger pay than the firemen and other benefits which these gentlemen did not receive at all. So far as the pay of the pilot is concerned, there is no comparison with the pay of the fire-fighters. I do not wish to labour the point any farther, but I think it would be just a matter of justice for the government to reconsider their attitude and exempt these men from income tax.

I would not want the committee to think that all the sympathy for the fire-fighters and the justice of their claim is on the other side of the house. I have had a great number of representations made to me by members of the fire-fighters. I also believe in the justice of their claim, but I believe sincerely that the Acting Minister of Finance has made a true statement when he says that the government had no agreement with the fire-fighters. It is tine that they are under the impression or they were under the impression that they would receive treatment similar to that to be received by members of the armed services. As I see it, we are only carrying on a long discussion, each repeating what the other said, and all stating that we believe in the justice of their claim. I believe the Acting Minister of Finance should consider allowing this item to stand. I think the fire-fighters are perhaps the most important organized, civilian group with a claim to be considered for exemption in regard to income tax. If other groups are organized and have similar claims, they Should also be considered on their merits. In these circumstances I would ask the minister whether he should not let the item stand.

There is, I believe, a resolution on the order paper giving notice of legislation respecting benefits to both supervisors and fire-fighters, and I had not anticipated that a debate of the general nature we have heard to-night would come up on the budget resolutions. Since it has developed, however, I want to say a word or two with 
respect to both the auxiliary services and the fire-fighters, only, however, in relation to the matter of income tax, which is germane to this resolution.
I was one of those who urged in the committee, and I am one of those who urge now in this committee of the whole, that as far as the auxiliary services are concerned they should receive the benefits which members of the armed forces received in the matter of income tax exemption. I am quite well aware that, at the time the order in council conferred upon the auxiliary services all the other benefits enjoyed by the armed forces, it specifically excluded income tax considerations. But a great deal has happened since that time. The committee believed,, as I believe, and now urge again upon the minister, that in regard to income tax they should be granted, in the terms of the recommendation of the committee, all the benefits which accrued to tihe armed forces, because to all intents and purposes they were members of the armed forces. It is perhaps fortunate that the Acting Minister of Finance is also Minister of National Defence and is himself a soldier, because, if he hears it, I think he will accept the validity of what I am about to say. The test of whether or not a man is serving as a member of the armed forces is the question of discipline: and we were informed on tihe authority of the officer commanding the corps at the time, and the officer who commanded the auxiliary services overseas, that they were amenable to all discipline and subject to court martial.
That being the case, it is difficult to distinguish between those in the armed forces and a group who follow the armed forces in all their operations, who are subject to exactly the same discipline and who receive the same rates of pay. They were in fact, Whether or not they were in theory, in the uniform of His Majesty's forces, though they did not wear the insignia of rank. I am well aware of the fact that technically it can be said they were not, but we recognized their position When in the beginning we granted them by order in council all other benefits except that in connection with the income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We did not do it in the beginning.
Well, it was very near the beginning.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
It was after this conference I mentioned, with the heads of the organizations.

Income War Tax

I do not have the exact dates. I have been through this so often I could almost recite it from memory, with the exception of the dates. In any event, the principle has been established, and there does not seem to be any great division of opinion.
I am perfectly well aware of the argument the minister has advanced to-night, that if you concede this treatment to one group which is, technically at least, civilian, you are opening the door to other groups.
The veterans committee did not recommend any other civilian groups except the supervisors and the fire-fighters.
I know that, but I have not yet reached the fire-fighters.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I think there was a recommendation that merchant seamen who became prisoners of war should receive income tax remission.
That is a different matter.
I do not propose to go through all twenty-four reports that were tabled^-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Thank goodness for that.
I would do so if I thought it necessary to bring the facts to the attention of hon. members.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think my hon. friend was right, and this discussion would be more appropriate under the resolution to which he referred.

Quite, and I propose, therefore, to confine my remarks to those aspects which touch on the income tax matter.
