I say again that I was and am one of those who urge that, having gone as far as we have by agreement with these auxiliary services, based particularly on the fact that they were completely amenable to military discipline including court martial, and based on the experience of the men at Hong Kong, we should concede this point.
Then we come to the second group which has been under discussion to-night, the firefighters. Again the veterans committee, both the main committee and the subcommittee of which I was a member, recommended with respect to income tax that the fire-fighters be granted not less favourable terms than those granted to any group that was specified. When the report of the subcommittee came in. the main committee amended' it to make it read "identical". It is the same thing, because, having recommended everything to one. if you give no less to another you give everything to both.
I rose primarily not to make my own position clear, because by now I think that is abundantly clear, but to point out to the committee and to those who may be following this debate that those who have been urging the claims of these two groups with respect to income tax are not speaking as a bloc or as a group but are, I think, representative of the majority of veteran opinion in this house.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: After listening to the hon. members who have spoken, I can say only ont thing. If I may paraphrase the words of Gilbert and Sullivan, it is evident that the lot of a minister of finance is not a happy one. He would like to be a good fellow, but he cannot be.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Would the Acting Minister of Finance tell us how many of these fire-fightets have paid this tax and how many have not paid it, out of the four hundred?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am afraid I would have to obtain that information. Those are figures, of course, coming within the department of my colleague the Minister of National Revenue, but perhaps they could be obtained.
I do not think any have paid.

I understand that last year they received back assessments for three years, and it was a shock to them. I do not believe any of them have paid. If you insist on this going through I believe that a great many of them will find themselves in definite financial difficulties.
There is just one more thing I should like to ask the minister. What other civilian groups who served overseas might become eligible if we recognized the claim of the fire-fighters?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I gave that information earlier; perhaps my hon. friend was out. He will find it in Hansard; there are five or six groups.
Could the minister give the aggregate number?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I can run over them again; I think I remember. There are the fire-fighters, the auxiliary services, the merchant marine, the ferry command, the test pilots, the civilian instructors in the flying schools; and other groups have put forward claims, including the deep sea fishermen. I think there were also some war correspondents who claimed they should have this status as well.

Who actually served in a theatre of war?
Income War Tax

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Or who claimed they were in danger areas, such as the deep sea fishermen who were in submarine infested waters off the eastern coast of Canada.
It seems to me that this is a matter which should be seriously investigated. I have been listening carefully-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We have taken an hour and a half on it, as we have every year to my knowledge _

I am not satisfied that what we are doing here is sufficient investigation. It has been said from the other side of the house that this item should be allowed to stand, and I am convinced that it should stand until we look into the matter further.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: My hon. friend realizes it does not come under this resolution we are considering. Strictly speaking, it is hardly in order.
Yes it does.

The allegation has been made that Major-General LaFleche made a certain statement-not once, but several times. He was a military man with some prestige. The statement is made that he does not recall having made those remarks. I have more faith in affidavits than has the Minister of National Revenue. There was submitted to the committee on veterans affairs an affidavit signed by thirty-eight persons to the effect that he did say it. An important principle is involved here. One cannot lightly pass it to one side. I am not satisfied, after a perusal of the affidavit, that it was a concoction. As a matter of fact it looks to me as if it was a bona fide attempt to tell the truth.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That has not been disputed.
Yes, it was disputed to-night. I believe the Minister of National Revenue said that he repudiated it, or words to that effect.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No, he never said that.

He said he challenged it, and Hansard will reveal that remark. There was a promise made. Either these men are not telling the truth, or Major-General LaFleche is guilty of false pretences. I cannot see it in any other way. It is a matter for serious reflection, and should be investigated. A man of his prominence and prestige should not make a statement like that unless he had some authority to make it. These men went overseas, and some of them did not come back. A few were wounded, and the families of some are to-day getting pensions. It seems 
to me that we pass too lightly over these things, and I suggest that we should investigate this matter and settle it for all time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: When did these firefighters leave for service overseas? Were they assessed for these taxes when they were overseas? If not, when were they assessed? I understand that the minister is not now in a position to say how many of them have paid.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
A comparatively small
number.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: How long were they in the service of the government without this assepment having been made? Perhaps the minister could give us some idea as to what the payments would be, after their having been in the service of the government for years, and the assessment having come only in recent months.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall have to get that information. It is not available here. I know, however, it would be only a comparatively small number who would be liable to tax, because those who were married with dependents would probably have bigger exemptions. It involves a very small group of men who would be liable to tax. But I will get the information the leader of the opposition has asked for, and try to give it to him to-morrow, or, at any rate, not later than w'hen we bring in the bill.

I endorse the suggestion made by the hon. member for Ottawa East, that this resolution be allowed to stand, and that the Acting Minister of Finance give it further consideration. It is not a question of asking him to make a good fellow of himself; nobody is asking that. It is a question of having an injustice remedied. The minister has said that if he lets one group in he is obliged to let them all in, and that it w'ould not be possible to pick and choose. May I point out to him, as I did in opening the discussion on the resolution, that the committee on veterans affairs have made that choice for him. Here we have a committee of sixty members of the house, everyone of whom served in one or other of the two great wars, and some in both.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I did, myself.
They have gone into this question thoroughly and at great length, with the result that the day before yesterday they brought in this recommendation which I shall read to the minister again.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am familiar with it.

They recommend:

Income War Tax
That the supervisors of the auxiliary service and fire-fighters of the Corps of Canadian Firefighters dispatched overseas, and members of the Canadian Red Cross Society and the St. John ambulance brigade who served in an actual theatre of war, be accorded all benefits, pensions. rehabilitation rights and income tax exemption as members of the armed forces.
I would ask that the minister allow the resolution to stand.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall gladly allow it to stand, and give it consideration. But I do not want to hold out any false hopes to the committee that it is likely the decision will be changed. Certainly, so far as I personally am concerned, I think it is more than doubtful. But we gladly allow the section to stand, because I do not want anyone to think I have a completely closed mind on the subject. I will consider it. May I say, however, that I have given this question the most earnest consideration for a matter of two or three years. It is not a new question to me, because I have previously given it most earnest and careful consideration.

Probably you made your
mind/ up two years ago; that is the trouble.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That is possible. But I
have made my mind up on other matters, and while I have sometimes changed it, I have not always done so.
Would the minister like to put it to a free vote of the committee?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am afraid the responsibility of deciding what tax exemptions will and what will not be granted, under the British system must remain the responsibility of the government of the day. My hon. friend knows that as well as I do. That is one way in which our system differs from other systems, including that of the United States. In Canada, the government must take the responsibility in matters of this kind. It is not an easy responsibility. A government could popularize itself with these various groups; but I have endeavoured to state the principle upon which this question of total exemption has been viewed. We have occupied an hour and forty minutes in discussing this question of firefighters, and I think the suggestion that we allow the resolution to stand is a good one.

Before the minister
allows it to stand-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I am in the hands of the
committee.	[DOT]

We are still in a
British country, and in such a country a minister of the crown is responsible to parliament. If a majority of members of parliament desire that a matter be changed, even though it be income tax it should be changed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is correct.

If it once becomes
thoroughly embedded in the minds of hon. members in the opposition that the government is determined to pay no attention to their desires, then members of the opposition will have to consider ways and means.
I wish to say a word or two respecting these fire-fighters, and would associate myself with *hon. members who have already spoken concerning them. I have been in contact with members of the fire-fighters, and I know positively that they were assured by General LaFleche, before they left this side, that they would be accorded all the rights and privileges of members of the armed services. I know that for certain. Then we proceed to collect arrears in taxes which the men did not know they owed! When a government calls upon a man to pay two or three years' arrears in taxes, or even one year's when he did not know he owed it, I believe that is worse than fining a man. It is as bad as the old capital levy for which they beheaded at least one king of England.
That matter is worthy of consideration. No government has any right to call upon a man for payment of arrears in taxes, when he did not know he was taxable.
Resolution stands.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Resolutions 19 and 20 stand.
28. That for 1946 and subsequent taxation years the provision under which the minister may allow double depreciation in respect of plant or equipment built or acquired as a new investment in a period to be fixed by the governor in council be amended to provide that the allowance be made only in respect of such classes of plant or equipment as may be determined by the governor in council.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Would the minister explain this resolution, and also state where in the act is to be found the provision that is being changed? Will he also give the committee some idea as to what classes of plant are no longer to get double depreciation and what classes of plant are to continue to get double depreciation?
Income War Tax

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The legislation which will be based on resolution 28 will bring into the law authority to define by order in council the classes of assets in respect of which double depreciation is granted under section 6 (1) (n) (ii) of the act, which reads:
(1) in computing the amount of the profits or gains to be assessed, a deduction shall not be allowed in respect of
(n) depreciation, except such amount as the minister in his discretion may allow, including
(ii) depreciation at not more than double the rates normally allowed in respect of plant or equipment built or acquired in a period to be fixed by the governor in council for the purposes of this paragraph, if the taxpayer is, in the opinion of the minister, making a new investment by building or acquiring the plant or equipment.
Hitherto the classes of assets have been defined by order in council under the authority of the War Measures Act, or, on its expiration, of the transitional powers act, and it is necessary to have continuing authority under the act itself. There will be no change in policy as a result of this amendment, since it merely provides authority for the continuation of the present practice. I am sorry that I have not a copy of the order in council, but the general classes excluded are commercial and business establishments as distinct from manufacturing and industrial establishments.
My hon. friend will recall that the purpose of the section was to encourage the building of new productive facilities during the reconstruction period. On the advice of the minister of reconstruction, it was narrowed down to the classes of assets of manufacturing plants to which I referred. My hon. friend will recall that the minister of reconstruction had to give a certificate to the Department of National Revenue. It might be more satisfactory if I were to have available a copy of the order in council as it now stands so that I could answer questions in detail.
If the committee would care to pass the resolution I would have the order in council available when the bill is brought in. In essence there is no change in the law. We are simply taking the law as it is, which was administered in part^by statute and in part by order in council under the War Measures Act which will lapse shortly after the commencement of the next session of parliament.
I think the matter is one of considerable importance. My recollection is that the measure has been both extended and restricted. I believe that it has been extended to shipbuilding.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is correct.
That it applies to ships, the approval for the construction of which has been given before December 1, 1947, and which will have been launched by March 31, 1948.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The approval must be given before March 31, 1947, and the work completed by March 31, 1948.
I understand there is some provision that if the work be not completed, priority is allowed on the work accomplished, provided that it has been authorized in the first place.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I believe that is right.

That has to do with extension but I think there have been some restrictions. In so far as I am acquainted with the matter, I am not critical of them, but I believe there is a lack of definition. There is still a vast field of discretion which I imagine will have to be restricted and defined by the statute. One of the questions which arises is whether new investment means new construction. In these days people are buying from War Assets Corporation plants which are costing huge sums of money and which undoubtedly are to be devoted to new purposes. They were used for the purpose of making munitions of war and in the future they will undoubtedly be devoted to the manufacture of peacetime commodities. Is such an investment one which would fall within the resolution, and would such a building, being a new investment, be subject to this double depreciation should the owner so optate?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: If the asset is within the order. I understand that the restrictions imposed by the order in council on the type of assets which are eligible for double depreciation represent a number of exclusions of assets used in service, distribution, communications and other non-manufacturing industries and also the exclusion of certain assets universally used, such as automobiles and trucks. In general, the double depreciation is granted on fixed assets employed in manufacturing industries. When I have before me a copy of the order in council I shall probably be able to deal more satisfactorily with the inquiries of the hon. member for Stanstead and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

If I had not encountered a slight mishap I would have been able to let the minister have a copy of the order in council. My filing system has failed because I changed my coat before coming into the chamber. Would it not be well to let the resolution stand because it is one of considerable importance?

Income War Tax

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Would my hon. friend allow the resolution to pass, and then he could bring up any changes which he might consider desirable to be incorporated when the bill is before us? All we are doing with_ this resolution is substituting statutory authority for the authority which now exists by virtue of an order in council under the War Measures Act. I do not want to press the point, but I do not believe the position of the house would be prejudiced by allowing the resolution to pass and discussing the matter in detail on the bill itself.
Would machinery and equipment which had been used for war purposes but which is being converted to peacetime uses be subject to this type of depreciation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am advised by the deputy minister that, subject to verification by looking at the order, the answer is yes.
The resolution refers to classes of plant or equipment as may be determined by the governor in council. Will that discretion be still reserved by the bill?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I understand that will still be reserved. This, as the committee will appreciate, is special incentive legislation, and I think it is the type of legislation in which some discretion is desirable in the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply or the governor in council. Questions of shortages of material and of labour are involved.

I should like to get some information, because the minister will recall that there 'have been serious clashes, shall I say, betvyeen different members of the ministry and great disappointment has resulted to people who thought they were beneficiaries of this principle. I think it is to the knowledge of some members opposite that the certificate of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply was not always honoured by another minister whose duty it was to see that abundant revenue was collected, and I should like to know if the principle has been refined to such an extent that these clashes of jurisdiction and the disappointment resulting therefrom will be precluded.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not know whether it would be correct to say that there has been a clash; but the ultimate authority, as my hon. friend knows, and will see by looking at the clause, rests with the Minister of National Revenue.

There was no doubt
where it rested. I think the gentleman who sits before the minister, never had any doubt
as to where it rested, but I was thinking of the unfortunate gentlemen who thought when they had the certificate of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply that they had something more than an illusion.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think every effort should be made to make the order in council as explicit as possible so that the possibility of clash will be minimized.

If the minister is still suggesting that this resolution should pass, I must say that I am not quite satisfied. Are we now to shift over from a situation where it was publicly known what classes were included to having a discretion exercised?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
We are not shifting over.
The. classes will be determined by order in council, that is true; but that order in council will be published. The only change which is being made here is a change in authority. The authority to pass the order in council to-day is conferred by the War Measures Act, but, if this resolution passes, the authority will be conferred by the Income War Tax Act. That is the only difference. There will be no difference in the way in which the order in council is issued, except in so far as the suggestion of the hon. member for Stanstead were followed. The order in council will be along the lines of the order in council which is issued now under the War Measures Act.

Let me persist with one question further. Will there in due course be made public the details referred to here, the classes of plant or equipment, so that it will be publicly known in respect of what classes this double depreciation operates?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
It is published now and
will be made public under the new order in council.

I am not sure that the
minister would feel that the present order in council makes it absolutely clear that eligibility depends upon the nature of the investment or upon the use to which the machinery or plant shall be put. That is a matter of some importance. If the minister could answer that question, I will not ask any more at this point.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I find it a little hard to
make the distinction, and so do the officials in front of me.

That is why I asked the question.
Income War Tax

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The nature of the investment will indicate the use to which it is put. If the investment is in a manufacturing plant I do not know that it would make very much difference whether the plant were making hairpins or some other commodity, nails or anything else.

It would make a lot
of difference if it were making nails just now.

I will not pursue the
question further this evening, but I hope that when the measure is brought down by the minister it will be such as to shed a broad light upon a most important measure which the investing public up to the moment has not had any opportunity of understanding very well.

We have heard a lot
about discretion in the last few days. I can understand the discretion of the minister in interpreting the act. Once that discretion is exercised, it becomes part of the very act itself. Will the legislation that is to be brought down give discretion to the minister as to who will get the benefit of this double depreciation? Will he have discretion to say that one person will get double depreciation and another person in the same business will not?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No, he cannot discriminate in that way.

Will the minister say
that wherever this discretion is exercised and somebody gets double depreciation, which is in the nature of a bonus, the facts will be made public? Is this to be kept secret as well as a man's income?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I would not think the names of individual taxpayers would be published, together with the amount of depreciation which - they have been granted. The so-called discretion of the minister is restricted to the question whether in his opinion the taxpayer is making a new investment by building or acquiring plant or equipment. He passes on that.
And having passed on it, does it become a matter of public knowledge?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The exercise of discretion which is made in the case of any taxpayer does not necessarily mean that the facts shall be made public. I would think that in most cases they would not be. I would think that parliament might ask, as was asked here to-day, how many cases there were in which 
special depreciation of this kind had been granted and how much the depreciation amounted to, but I would not think it proper to disclose the exact investment of the individual taxpayer. I am thinking aloud, but that is the view I take.

I am going to ask the minister this final question. He may recall that yesterday I became a little bit agitated because I was, as I thought, being coerced into something. Will a person making this type of investment be forced to take the double depreciation if he does not want to?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The answer is no. It may be to his advantage to spread the depreciation forward.
He still has the option.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It seems to me that one of the points the hon. member for Stanstead is making is valid, namely, that the purpose of the plant has some signfieance. As I recall, the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply the other day referred to the decision of the government to continue double depreciation for plants engaged in producing materials required in the construction of homes, which is a matter of considerable social importance at the present time. It is along that line that I suggest that the act itself should contain some of the principles at present in the order in council, which has been in existence for some time. The government has had experience and knows all the facts, and I would hope that it might be more specific in the legislation than appears to be the case at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I will take into consideration the suggestion which the hon. member and others have made along the same line.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
This is perhaps a complicated provision. The legislation to be based on this resolution relates to the provisions which were announced in the 1944 budget dealing with deferred maintenance and repairs. It will be recalled that at that time an amendment was enacted to allow one-half the expenditures incurred in a period to be designated by the governor in council to be charged against the income of a previous fiscal period ending in a year not earlier than 1943. As yet the period in which expenditures incurred would be eligible under this provision has not been named, and the purpose of the legislation to be based on the resolution is to restrict the application of this carry-back when it becomes effective to income that was subject to tax at the rate applying to excess profits in the years 1943 to 1946. As the committee will understand, the flat rate of corporation income tax will be reduced by the budget proposals from 40 to 30 per cent and the excess profits tax rate from 20 to 15 per cent, effective January 1, 1947.
It will be immediately apparent, therefore, that any corporation paying only the 30 per cent rate of corporation tax in the future would automatically gain by carrying back an expenditure to a previous year when it paid only the minimum 40 per cent rate of combined tax. I would point out also that this gain would arise solely because the naming of the period in which the expenditures are eligible may be incurred, concerning which I wish to make a statement later on, has been delayed to a time later than was contemplated when this legislation was introduced in 1944.
I would also point out that the case for this measure was argued at a time when the 100 per cent rate of excess profits tax was in effect and that profits subject to this tax were asserted to be artificially high in many businesses because the normal costs for maintenance and repairs, impossible to undertake during war time, were missing.
I believe I am correct in saying that it was . never in the government's mind that companies not subject to the excess profits tax rate would in general benefit from this special carry-back provision; and I may add that
when I used the term "excess profits tax rate" I refer to the 100 per cent rate and the 60 per cent rate of last year.
We are, however, now faced with a situation in which many companies which have never paid the excess profits tax rate would receive a benefit owing to the necessity placed on the government, in fulfilling this obligation under the wartime tax agreements with the provinces, of reducing its corporation tax by ten per cent. Such companies would receive benefits which were never intended at the time the legislation was introduced and which would not arise except for the unforeseen necessity of postponing the period for an indefinite time. In the light of the above circumstances, it is proposed that the benefit of this provision, when it comes into operation, shall be limited to those business concerns which have paid tax under the rate applicable to excess profits.
I should like the committee and the business community at large to appreciate the difficult position in which the government has found itself in regard to the question of naming the period required to give effect to this measure. On the one hand, we have been pressed by businesses which have found it impossible to postpone their rehabilitation programmes any longer, asking us to name the period immediately in order that their expenditures may qualify; and, on the other hand, because of the serious shortage of materials and equipment, we have been pressed to delay the period until more ample supplies will allow business generally to receive the maximum advantage from its operation.
The government itself has also been faced with the responsibility of avoiding as far as possible any action that would place an additional strain on the acute situation with respect to building materials and accentuate shortages which have already seriously interfered with the housing programme in particular.
While the government has realized that in circumstances where it has been impossible further to postpone maintenance and repair expenditures deferred during war years, the fact that the period has not yet been named will mean a loss of benefit which would have been available were the period now in effect, it has not regarded it as in the general public interest to take any step which would place any added strain on the supply situation.
This matter, I may say, has been under review from time to time and will continue to be given constant consideration, but I regret that it is not yet deemed expedient to bring this measure into effect, nor is it pos-
Income War Tax

sible in the present outlook to give any assurance as to when it will be proclaimed, apart from the assurance that it will be delayed no longer than is necessitated by the exigencies of the supply situation.

I understand that this measure, which is splendidly complicated in its language, is not actually in effect and the period has not been named in which it is likely to come into effect. I have a suggestion to make to the minister with regard to mining in particular. Owing to the condition of the structures of the mines in Canada, particularly the workings underground, many mines have during the war done practically no exploration and have been in many ways seriously depleted when there was a tremendous demand for metal for production. The normal processes of mining were not carried on; probably the normal processes of a great many other businesses were in the same condition, and the structures and physical assets of the companies were not kept up in the way in which they should have been under normal business practice. I realize the difficulty the minister has in proclaiming a set period. What would be wrong with having the period optional to each individual concerned? Would that produce a chaotic situation. Some of the companies need the relief probably sooner than others. Some are now facing a critical situation in consequence of their depleted and deteriorated physical structures. Would it not be possible to allow some of the companies to take a period which was optional to them?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I shall look into the question raised by my hon. friend. As he will appreciate, the legislation recognizes the fact that concerns which were earning high profits were unable to make their normal maintenance and repairs. By reason of that fact their profits were greater than they would otherwise be. The thought behind the legislation was that in a period shortly after the war it would be desired to stimulate production, encourage the making of these repairs, and that the government would then fix a period when the supply situation was such as to enable that to be done without interfering with other national activities, and that the benefit could then be taken back into the years referred to in the act. Whether it would be possible to make it optional or not with the individual company, I will not say at the moment, but I think it unlikely. As matters stand at present, I do not need to tell hon. members that materials and labour generally are in short supply and that, therefore, this is not the time when we want to encourage the making of these expenditures.
[Mr. Abbott.1

I realize that this is not the time to encourage the making of these expenditures, but a number of industries are being driven to a more and more deteriorated state, and their efficiency is suffering because of the deteriorated state into which their plant has fallen.
I gather that the resolution affects only concerns or corporations which were paying the excess profits tax when it was 100 per cent. Is that not right?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is right, or when it was 60 per cent.
But it will not affect concerns which pay the excess profits tax under the present-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Not concerns which paid what I might loosely describe as the normal rate of 40 per cent.

It is difficult to say how many mines will be affected at the present time, some of which definitely went out and practised extremely bad mining practice in which they just took out their high-grade ore, and now find themselves in an extremely bad condition. When production was necessary they mined their high-grade veins and left their low-grade veins behind, and in some cases made really abnormal profits.
If the minister will look at the profits statement of a great many corporations in the last year he will find a considerable decrease in the profits made by many corporations, particularly mining corporations. I am not speaking now of the recent effect of parity; I am speaking of the conditions which accrued even before parity, because some of the mines have been forced to go back and put their properties into shape in order to carry on their business. Profits have fallen considerably, and I point out to the minister that in an operation such as mining these repairs or this rehabilitation of property must go on in order that the mine may continue. I assume that a great number of other concerns must be placed in the same position. Take a concern which has a steam boiler which has been used during the war and is still being used, but perhaps is not as safe as it should be. In a case like that, the concern should be given an opportunity to appeal or make its case optional before the government. There is every possibility that the building situation, the material situation, and the steel situation will get worse rather than better. We have to look at that. Perhaps I realize that better than anybody in the committee because I am trying to build a house at the present time. Therefore I know what the situation with regard to building material

really is. There are many concerns in Canada to-day which find themselves definitely in a critical situation with regard to their physical plant, and some consideration should be given to making this resolution and the period when it becomes operative optional, and to give these concerns which find themselves, in common parlance, behind the eight ball, an opportunity of getting relief.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
As my hon. friend has pointed out, this resolution affects only those concerns which are in the 100 per cent excess profits tax bracket, or which paid excess profits taxes at the rate of 60 per cent. I am told that it would not affect many gold mines, because there rvere almost none in that category, although I have no doubt that there were some base metal mines.
I shall give consideration to the points raised by the hon. member, but I think it would be most undesirable to attempt to put it on a basis of selectivity or to try to give the minister the discretion to decide which company should get it and at which period. However, I shall give consideration to the points which have been raised by the hon. member for York West.

I have a question that I want to ask, but before asking it may I say that I believe that a number of base metal mines find themselves in a difficult position because they responded, as the hon. member for York West has said, to the great demand for base metals. They took out the ore of the higher grades and did great damage to the mine as a business. There is something comparable to repairs which have to be made before a mine can be operated effectively and economically. I do not see any provision in the resolutions for that damage wThich was done for other than business reasons. The chief and only inspiration to do as the mine owners did. was to increase production, which meant nothing to them, because, as the minister has said, many of them were in the categories wherein 100 per cent of their profits were taxable. Has any provision been made for the rehabilitation of these great sources of employment and wealth?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I agree with what my hon. friend has said, that a great many of these base metal mines did accelerate production, and by doing so did accelerate the depreciation of the plant and equipment. There were a number of cases in which special agreements were made with mines for the crown to grant them accelerated depreciation, but other than that there is no special provision. As I pointed out in my remarks a little earlier, the government realizes there are cases in which
it will be impossible for certain manufacturers or mine operators further to postpone the making of long-deferred maintenance repairs and replacements. As I also said, that will mean a loss of benefit to these firms; but it is still felt that, in the interests of the public generally and the manufacturers generally who would be entitled to avail themselves of this, the time has not yet come when a period can be designated within which expenditures for such deferred maintenance and repairs can be availed of as a charge back to previous years.

I wanted to ask this
question, dealing with a large class of companies whose operations were almost suspended during the war. They did nothing, or practically nothing; they earned no profits or in any event not sufficient profits to maintain their equipment. Now that business has come back, they find themselves confronted with this difficulty. Either they must not accept work or they must buy new equipment, which is not going to be provided for by depreciation or anything of that kind. I am speaking now of equipment which has stood idle for five or six or seven years. I shall give the minister a typical company of the kind I have in mind, a road building company. They have done nothing; their equipment has rusted and rotted. To-day the work comes in and the equipment has to be renewed. How are they to do it? It will not be a proper charge against earnings, and I do not find anything in the act or in the resolutions to meet that situation. It seems to me that this is a practical question and one of which the deputy has had probably a number of instances placed before him.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That, of course, is perfectly true, as no one knows better than my hon. friend; but depreciation is only of value to a taxpayer if he has profits against which to write off the depreciation. I have no doubt the road building companies are an excellent example of concerns whose plant and equipment depreciated during the war period, when there w'ere no earnings against which depreciation could be written off. But as far as I know there is nothing in the law which would allow them to take depreciation to-day which they could have taken in previous years, and I do not think there is any intention of introducing such a provision. This measure, as my hon. friend knows, and as I indicated earlier, w*as intended to help the man whose profits were svmllen if anything by reason of the fact that he was not able to make normal maintenance and repairs; to enable him to make them at a later date and charge them back into that period of very high taxation.
Income War Tax

But to promote employment I thought it might be a matter of policy which the government would like to explore. If the replacement of this machinery could be made a first- charge upon profits up to an amount which the government might think reasonable, I am sure it would promote business activity and employment and the general well-being of large sections of the community.

I was very glad to hear that in the past there were some companies who did not manage to spend considerable sums out. of their excess profits instead of the money going to the government. I did not know that such companies existed. But I cannot see why a company that had excess profits would not write off depreciation. No doubt they did write it off, and they have that depreciation in their hands right now. It is real money.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I had better clear up this point. We did get into a discussion of depreciation, but this section has nothing to do with depreciation. This relates to deferred maintenance, what would have been ordinary operating, expenses of the concern and chargeable as such, but which they were not able to make because of the shortage of materials or shortage of labour or otherwise.
But I was going to get into the question of depreciation anyway; the hon. member for Stanstead was holding me back.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Having allowed the hon.
member for Stanstead to speak on it, I suppose I must allow my hon. friend to do so, though it is not under this resolution.

I am not speaking
about mines. I do not know anything about them except that they are things you get money out of and things some people put money into which they never get back. I am speaking of this broad section. As I understand it, you are only going to allow any money they will spend in the future out of the excess profits the government got out of them in the good years, when they had swollen profits. If they did not have profits, then depreciation was not allowed. Depreciation is written off because some day you are going to have to replace the capital structure, or some part of it, and for that you use this depreciation, which is actually money in your hands. Then, what other concession should they have than the privilege of using this money which they kept back from the government and have in their hands to-day? If

you start giving back 100 per cent excess profits I think you should do so in such a way that everyone would get his share. Under the Excess Profits Tax Act a small business was prevented from making any advance at all because of the low base. Those people from whom you took excess profits equal to perhaps five or six times their whole capital structure should receive some consideration. I should like the minister to explain why the companies the government is going to help are the companies that had excess profits and the companies that have in their hands the depreciation with which to make the necessary repairs.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I shall be glad to do what I can to explain to my hon. friend the point he has raised, though, if he will allow me to say so, it has nothing to do with this resolution, which relates to a provision that has been on the statute books since 1944. As I explained in my opening statement, this regulation made provision for the case of the concern which during the war years was not able to make its normal, ordinary maintenance expenditures. Companies of that kind, who thereby had their profits increased beyond what they would have been under ordinary normal business practice, can do that later. Take the case of a concern-
The railways.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I shall take a smaller
example. Take a concern which normally would earn 850,000 a year and which normally would spend $10,000 in regular, proper repairs and maintenance.	During the war years,
because of shortage of materials and labour shortage, it was not able to spend that $10,000. What was the effect? Its profits were increased from 850,000 to S60.000. Ordinarily, if it could have obtained the materials or the men it would have made those everyday, regular, normal repairs. It could not do that, so that its profits were artificially increased, if I may so describe it, by reason of those circumstances. It was recognized that there was a hardship there, and we said to those companies, "If you make those deferred maintenance and repairs after the period of scarcity is over, in a period which is designated by the government, we will allow you to charge them, to the extent of one half, back into those years, from 1943 to 1946 when you would normally have made them." That is all.
Under the proposed resolution we restrict that privilege, if I may call it that, to taxpayers that were big profit earners during the period of the war, companies which, as I said, were in the 100 per cent bracket, or who paid the 60 per cent rate. The only difficulty wre

Income War Tax
are in at the present time is that, because of the shortage of materials and of labour which still exists, we cannot designate a period yet within which those who are eligible may avail themselves of that right. It has nothing whatever to do with depreciation.
Mr. MeMASTER: I do not see how it can be dissociated from depreciation. The income tax branch will disallow everything that is not ordinary repairs. The cost of other than ordinary repairs is taken out of depreciation account. If they7 do not spend it there, there will be the usual allowance for depreciation. They get the same benefit by depreciation that they would have got by spending the money on what are capital repairs, and the money allowed for depreciation is still in their hands.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The answer is no. My hon. friend should appreciate that one cannot take out of depreciation reserve expenditures for maintenance and repairs. Expenditures for maintenance and repairs are current operating charges. Amounts which are set aside in depreciation reserve are a capital charge. They are a charge against profit, it is true, but they are set up in a depreciation reserve in order to provide a return of capital to the taxpayer. On the other hand, expenditures for maintenance and repairs are current day-to-day, week-to-week, month-to-month, year-to-year operating expenses.
Mr. MeMASTER:	Even machinery is
lepreciated on a basis allowed by the department. They cannot go and buy new machinery or repair it, except through this depreciation fund; at least the income tax officials never allowed my clients to do so.

What bothers me is that it seems to me- and I am going back to the suggestion made by the hon. member for York West-that it might be done at a time to be chosen by the company; because as the minister has indicated, the relief they propose to give is limited to a certain time, and it is by no means certain that a company will be able to take advantage of it in that time. That will depend, as I see it, upon the circumstances of each particular company. If, as pointed out by the minister, this is advantageous, I am not clear as to why it need necessarily be confined wholly to the 100 per cent or 60 per cent excess profits tax company.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Because, as I said in my preliminary statement, it was never intended to benefit any other taxpayer. The justification for it, as my hon. friend will see if he looks at the debates, was that the companies
in question were in effect having taken away from them 100 per cent of amounts which otherwise they would have expended on maintenance and repairs.
Mr. MeMASTER: Would the minister give us the section of the act where that is indicated?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Yes, it is section 5 (v) which says:
In respect of income for a taxation year ending between the last day of December, one thousand nine hundred and forty-two and the first day of the year of expenditure, not more than one-half of expenditures made
(i)	in connection with maintenance and repairs by a taxpayer carrying on a business, or

That is to be amended in the way indicated in the resolution now before the committee.

One thing more. Our hypothetical company makes $50,000 a year and puts $10,000 into normal operating repairs. Now it makes $60,000. The $10,000 is 100 per cent gone; the government has got it. Now their machinery is depleted, and they are in a mess. I am not clear as to how exactly they will take the recoup for the expenditure of the $10,000 for three or four years-and incidentally it will perhaps be more than that, because of present increased prices. How do they get it back? What is the machinery for getting that back?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I would say that $5,000 of the $10,000 could be carried back into 1943, and charged there. In other words, the company's return would be reopened for 1943, and it would get an appropriate refund of taxes.
But not in 1942.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, and to provide:
1.	That the provision for taxation of excess profits of every person residing or ordinarily resident in Canada be amended to exclude tnere-irom in respect of excess profits earned after December 31. 1946, persons other than corporations nr joint stock companies and to reduce the rate of tax on excess profits earned after December 31, 1946. from 20 per cent to 15 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The first resolution proposes two things, first, that the rate of tax on excess profits earned after December 31, 1946 be reduced from 20 per cent to 15 per cent and, second, it exempts completely from the excess profits tax the profits of partnerships and sole proprietors as from January 1. 1947.
The second resolution repeals the flat rate tax on total profits as distinct from the rate of tax on excess profits with respect to earnings of 1947. At present the tax on total profits under the Excess Profits Tax Act is 22 per cent which, together with the IS per cent under the Income War Tax Act, makes the 40 per cent fiat rate. Concurrent with the repeal of this 22 per cent rate, the 18 per cent rate is being increased to 30 per cent. These two amendments taken together give effect to the undertaking under the provincial wartime agreements that the dominion would reduce the tax on corporate incomes by ten per cent of such income.
The third resolution provides for a minor amendment dealing with investment trusts and is in line with the amendments in connection with the Income War Tax Act. It
giants exemption from excess profits tax to all investment trusts, regardless of whether or not they have bonds outstanding. At present the exemption is limited to those who do not have bonds outstanding, and this is to give comparable treatment to the two classes of trust.
My understanding is that it remains indefinite; in other words, it continues from the end of 1946, the only difference being that it is 15 per cent instead of 20 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is correct.
I should like to draw attention to one or two things.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Sole proprietors and partnerships are out.

I want to refei to just one or two things said by the minister last October and again this year. I am referring to this matter purely as an employment measure. The Minister of Finance said that we should not rely too much on employment remaining as it is now, that we should think of everything that would possibly stimulate employment. I think that is generally recognized, and I wish to quote the minister on the point that the great objection to the 100 per cent excess was that it put no premium on efficiency. In fact, it almost put a premium on inefficiency. The Minister of Finance is reported on page 1004 of Hansard of October 12, 1945, as follows:
The Excess Profits Tax Act is a war measure which has commanded overwhelming support as an important and necesary instrument of war finance. Unmodified, it seriously weakens the stimulus toward the investment of capital and the efficient operation of enterprises. In this period of reconstruction it is becoming a barrier to expanding employment.
As reported later on the same page, the minister said:
There is widespread evidence that incentive is being stifled and that ordinary prudence in the making of business expenditures has been seriously weakened.
Speaking on June 17 of this year, as reported on page 2919 of Hansard, the minister said this:
I had hoped to be able to announce in this budget the repeal of the Excess Profits Tax Act in its entirety, effective as of January 1, 1947. As I explained last year, this tax was designed as a war measure and has received overwhelming support as a necessary instrument of war finance, but it has distinct weaknesses and limitations in normal times and is not to be accepted as a permanent part of our tax structure.
Excess Profits Tax

Then the minister went on to give as his reason for not dealing with it, which to me is one of the most unconvincing statements I have ever heard from the Minister of Finance:
Experience, however, has shown that we are still living in highly abnormal times, the shadow of the war is stfll upon us, and as I have shown the financial burdens on the dominion budget arising out of the war are still of huge proportions. After careful consideration the government has reached the conclusion that the act should stay on the statute books for another year unless provision is made at the next session of parliament for its earlier repeal.
I want to emphasize that I am talking about this as an employment measure. I know I am running the risk of some saying, "Oh, you are thinking of the corporations." I am just using the minister's words which, I think, are wise and sound1. I contend that the conclusion which the government has arrived at is entirely contrary to all the argument made by the minister, and I think it is a great mistake.

I am glad my hon.
friend very properly emphasized the word "unmodified" when he quoted the minister's speech.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: There are two comments I should like to make. First, despite what the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario has just said. I cannot but recall how rapidly the Excess Profits Tax Act has been modified since the end of the war as compared with the deaf ear we get when we try to plead the cause of personal income taxpayers in the lower brackets.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
We have gone over that before, but we can go over it again if it is thought desirable. One has to take the total economy into consideration. One has to consider the entire tax set-up; the situation in Britain, the shortages they have because of what they went through in the war, and the social security measures that have been brought down in that country. I am suggesting that we do what my hon. friends have proposed time and again, namely, make comparisons within our own country and on the basis of what is possible here. And what does seem obvious here is that this government in the_space of two years is able to bring about drastic modifications in the excess profits tax as compared with the modifications we have had in the personal income tax.

The other thing I would suggest is this. The Minister of Finance in his budget speech made reference in his closing paragraph to the general belief that we as Canadians can do just as great things in time of peace as we did in time of war. I suggest that there is a sense in which our objectives are parallel, namely, high production, and part of the way to achieve high production is to make sure that the results of production are put to social use. That comes about, not by facilitating the piling up of huge profits, but by using such instruments as are at our command to distribute properly wealth. On that basis the government has already gone far enough, if not too far, in the reductions it has made in this particular tax.

The minister, in making his reply in the budget debate, mentioned that some on this side-and I think he had reference to myself among others-had said that the retention of this excess profits tax, even though it is lowered slightly, was a great discouragement to production. He attacked that contention; and after reviewing the situation in Canada, where we have 30 per cent normal tax, and 5 per cent likely to be added by the provinces, and then 15 per cent excess profits tax, giving 50 per cent altogether-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
No; 15 per cent on the excess over 116% of standard, not on all profits. That is an important difference. It is not 50
per cent on all profits.
The basic rate is-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
Where the province imposes a tax the tax is 35 per cent on profits up to 116% of standard and 15 per cent on the excess. In most cases that would work out at
an average rate of about 38 per cent.

That is the mistake which I believe the Minister and his advisers have fallen into. What I am suggesting is that on the excess profits-define them as you like, 100 per cent or 116%-the effective tax rate will be 50 per cent. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is correct, but only on the excess. On 116% of standard the tax will be 30 or 35 per cent.

In this country it will be 50 per cent as against 38 per cent in the United States, and a still smaller rate on the smaller corporations, which fact the minister did not mention. The two examples I gave the minister were these. A company in the United States having a branch plant in Canada can arrange to do its export business from the parent plant across the line, or it can do its export business from its branch in Canada. If it does

Privilege-Mr. Coldwell
so much business, we will call it X, in the United States, and it also does X business in Canada, there is still its foreign trade business, which is additional to the ordinary business carried on domestically in both countries. If that company finds that the tax rate in the United States is 38 per cent on the foreign end of the business, and that the tax rate in Canada is 50 per cent, it is quite obvious where the business is going to be done.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: It cannot be 50 per cent in Canada.
It can be and you have just admitted it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Only on a relatively small proportion of the profits.

That is where the minister and his advisers make their cardinal mistake. I am not suggesting what the general rate of taxation is. All I am interested in is in getting the additional business. I am not think-about the average business but about the additional business, and the rate of taxation on that additional business is 50 per cent in Canada, whereas in the United States the rate remains at the flat corporation rate, which we will take as 38 per cent. So that there is no question where the additional business is going to be done. If, not the average business, but the additional business is produced in the United States the rate of taxation is 38 per cent. If the additional business is done here the rate is 50 per cent. It seems to me clear that the minister and his advisers have fallen into a complete lack of business foresight in not grasping that the average rate is of no consequence in regard to the extra foreign business we are trying to get. It is the rate on the last unit of business which counts, the rate here in Canada as against the rate in the United States, and I am saying that there is a twelve per cent differential, that the retained profit is twelve per cent higher in the United States and therefore the additional business is certainly going to be done there.
I mentioned also the example of a Canadian company', a great friend of the government, which was endeavouring to do some export business to Newfoundland and had the trade pretty well lined up. Then an American competitor came in and, because he had a larger retained profit, he was able to quote a closer price and get the business. We are not interested in the average tax rate on all the business of a Canadian company. That is all right for theorists to be interested in, but not practical business men who, if they have an opportunity to do additional business through a United States plant or a Canadian plant and the rate in the case of the United 63260-246
States plant is 38 per cent and in the case of the Canadian plant 50 per cent, will certainly have it done in the United States. The result of this retention of the excess profits tax on our Canadian economy, perhaps not so much now when we have employment and are doing fairly well in production, but in the future will be to deprive our manufacturers of just what is required in the way of incentive and providing employment for our people.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in.
